instruction: Please implement a website for generating stock reports to provide stock information and analysis. The website should have the functionality to search and summarize stock information, and generate customized stock reports based on user requirements. Users should be able to input stock codes or names, select report formats and content, and the website will automatically generate the corresponding reports. The reports should include basic stock information, market trends, financial data, and more. Set the background color to white and the component color to navy.

ui_instruct.task: Verify the stock search functionality by entering a valid stock code.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The system returns relevant stock information and analysis corresponding to the entered stock code, displaying details such as basic stock information, market trends, and financial data.

ui_instruct.task: Test the report customization feature by selecting different report formats and content options.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The system provides options for various report formats and content customization, enabling users to choose according to their preferences.

ui_instruct.task: Input a stock name instead of a stock code to search for stock information.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website successfully recognizes the stock name, retrieving and displaying the relevant stock information and analysis.

ui_instruct.task: Generate a customized stock report by choosing specific elements to include (e.g., market trends, financial data).
ui_instruct.expected_result: The generated report correctly includes the selected elements, accurately reflecting the user's specified choices.

ui_instruct.task: Navigate through the website and test all buttons function correctly by clicking each of them and back to the homepage.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Each click on a button leads to the appropriate page or action without any errors, ensuring smooth navigation.

ui_instruct.task: Evaluate the website's form inputs by submitting incomplete or incorrect stock information.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The system displays appropriate error messages and guidance on how to correct the input errors, ensuring robust input validation.

ui_instruct.task: Verify that the website uses 'white' as the background color and 'navy' as the component color, as specified in the design requirements.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website has a background color of 'white' and components (such as buttons, cards, headers, etc.) are styled with the color 'navy', accurately reflecting the design instruction.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Report users track the same tickers daily; a persistent watchlist is the natural home base that every later monitoring feature can hang off.
follow_ups.instruction: The report tool is great, but I need a home base - add a watchlist page where my stocks stay in view and I can add or remove entries as I go. Start me off with exactly these seven, I'll grow it later: Comet Semiconductors (CMET, Technology, $91.75, +2.4% today, P/E 45.0, dividend yield 0.5%), Dune Foods (DUNE, Consumer, $34.60, -0.8%, P/E 15.3, 2.8%), Atlas Robotics (ATLS, Technology, $142.50, +2.4%, P/E 38.2, no dividend), Everglade Utilities (EVRG, Utilities, $67.10, +0.3%, P/E 11.8, 5.2%), Flint Financial (FLNT, Financials, $103.40, -1.2%, P/E 9.4, 3.6%), Glacier Health (GLCR, Healthcare, $76.25, +1.6%, P/E 22.7, 1.9%), and Brookwater Energy (BRKW, Energy, $58.20, -1.2%, P/E 12.6, 4.1%). Sort it by today's change with the biggest gainer on top, and whenever two stocks tie on any number - that goes for everything we build in this app from here on out - break the tie alphabetically by ticker. I also want a little summary strip counting gainers versus losers, a toggle that regroups the list by sector, and a button on each row that drops me into the report generator with that stock already filled in. One more house rule for the whole app, now and for anything we add later: dollars always with a $ sign and exactly two decimals, percentages with one decimal and an explicit + or - in front.

ui_instruct.task: Open the watchlist page and read the row order from top to bottom.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The rows read ATLS, CMET, GLCR, EVRG, DUNE, BRKW, FLNT - ATLS sits above CMET and BRKW above FLNT because the +2.4% and -1.2% ties break alphabetically by ticker; a build that keeps the seeded entry order would wrongly show CMET before ATLS and FLNT before BRKW.

ui_instruct.task: Look at the summary strip on the watchlist page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: It counts 4 gainers and 3 losers, matching the seven seeded stocks (ATLS, CMET, GLCR, EVRG up; DUNE, BRKW, FLNT down).

ui_instruct.task: Click the group-by-sector toggle on the watchlist.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The list regroups by sector with the Technology group containing exactly ATLS and CMET and each of the other five stocks under its own sector; clicking the toggle again restores the single change-sorted list.

ui_instruct.task: On the GLCR (Glacier Health) watchlist row, click its report button.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The report generator opens with GLCR / Glacier Health already filled in and produces that stock's report without the tester retyping the stock.

ui_instruct.task: Use the search input to look up a stock by code or name and generate a report with the default options.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A report is generated that includes a basic stock information section, market trends, and a financial data section.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Investors reading these reports still size trades by gut feel; a live risk-based position sizer turns the analysis into an actionable share count.
follow_ups.instruction: Next, I keep sizing trades on gut feel - give me a position size calculator page. I type four things - account balance, the percent of it I'm willing to risk, entry price, and stop-loss price - and it works out my dollar risk, how many shares to buy, and the total position cost, recalculating live with every keystroke rather than waiting for some button. Shares are whole numbers, always rounded down: $25,000 at 2% risk with a $58.20 entry and a $55.00 stop should read $500.00 risk, 156 shares (not 156.25), and a $9,079.20 position. And if I fat-finger a stop that isn't below the entry, don't show me nonsense numbers - just tell me the stop has to be below the entry.

ui_instruct.task: On the position size calculator, type 25000 for account balance, 2 for risk percent, 58.20 for entry price, and 55.00 for stop-loss.
ui_instruct.expected_result: It shows $500.00 dollar risk, 156 shares (rounded down - not 156.25 and not 157), and a $9,079.20 position cost.

ui_instruct.task: With 25000 / 2 / 58.20 / 55.00 entered, change the risk percent field from 2 to 4.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The outputs update immediately as the field changes, with no submit or generate step: $1,000.00 risk, 312 shares, $18,158.40 position cost.

ui_instruct.task: Enter 25000 for account balance, 2 for risk percent, 50.00 for entry, and 60.00 for stop-loss.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A message says the stop-loss has to be below the entry price, and no share count or position cost is presented as a valid result.

ui_instruct.task: Enter 10000 account balance, 1 risk percent, 20.00 entry, and 19.00 stop-loss, then read the dollar outputs.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Every dollar figure carries a $ sign and exactly two decimals - $100.00 risk and a $2,000.00 position - following the app-wide money format.

ui_instruct.task: Open the watchlist page and read the row order from top to bottom.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The rows read ATLS, CMET, GLCR, EVRG, DUNE, BRKW, FLNT - ATLS sits above CMET and BRKW above FLNT because the +2.4% and -1.2% ties break alphabetically by ticker; a build that keeps the seeded entry order would wrongly show CMET before ATLS and FLNT before BRKW.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Watchlist users care most about levels being crossed; a rules-plus-triggered alerts flow is the obvious next monitoring milestone on top of the watchlist.
follow_ups.instruction: Now price alerts. I want a spot where I pick any stock off my watchlist, choose above or below, type a target price, and it joins my active rules list - plus a separate triggered section showing which rules the current watchlist prices have already crossed, where above and below mean strictly past the line. Seed three for me: GLCR above $75.00 (already hit, it's at $76.25), DUNE below $34.60 (sitting exactly at the line, so not hit), and ATLS above $150.00 (nowhere close). Also a habit I want everywhere in this app from now on: anything deletable - alerts, watchlist rows, whatever comes later - asks me to confirm before it actually goes.

ui_instruct.task: Open the alerts area and look at the triggered section.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Exactly one rule shows as triggered - GLCR above $75.00; the DUNE below $34.60 rule is NOT triggered because DUNE sits exactly at $34.60 and above/below are strictly past the line, so a build using at-or-below would wrongly show two.

ui_instruct.task: Create a new alert: pick ATLS from the stock picker, choose below, type 100.00 as the target, and add it.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The new rule appears in the active rules list but not in the triggered section, since ATLS trades at $142.50 which is not below $100.00.

ui_instruct.task: Click delete on the ATLS above $150.00 alert and accept the confirmation.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A confirmation is requested before anything is removed; after confirming, that rule leaves the active list while the GLCR and DUNE rules remain.

ui_instruct.task: Add an alert for BRKW, above, with target 58.00.
ui_instruct.expected_result: It lands directly in the triggered section, because the watchlist prices BRKW at $58.20 which is strictly above $58.00 - the alert is evaluated against the watchlist's price.

ui_instruct.task: On the position size calculator, type 25000 for account balance, 2 for risk percent, 58.20 for entry price, and 55.00 for stop-loss.
ui_instruct.expected_result: It shows $500.00 dollar risk, 156 shares (rounded down - not 156.25 and not 157), and a $9,079.20 position cost.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Watching stocks naturally becomes owning them; a lot-level portfolio marked to watchlist prices gives these users real P/L accounting, not just quotes.
follow_ups.instruction: I actually own some of these, so add a portfolio page that marks my positions to the watchlist's current prices. My real lots: 20 shares of ATLS bought at $120.00 plus another 10 at $150.00 - fold those into a single ATLS line at the share-weighted average cost, which works out to $130.00, not the $135.00 you'd get by just averaging the two prices - then 50 BRKW at $62.00 and 40 EVRG at $60.50. Each line should show shares, average cost, market value, gain or loss in dollars and percent, and that position's percent of the whole portfolio, with a totals row at the bottom. If the math's right that comes out to $9,869.00 total value and +$449.00 overall.

ui_instruct.task: Open the portfolio page and look at the ATLS line.
ui_instruct.expected_result: There is one consolidated ATLS row (not two separate lots) showing 30 shares at an average cost of $130.00 - the share-weighted figure, not the $135.00 a naive average of the two buy prices gives - with market value $4,275.00.

ui_instruct.task: Read the totals row on the portfolio page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Total market value is $9,869.00 and overall gain is +$449.00, with the overall percent shown to one decimal as +4.8%.

ui_instruct.task: Compare the BRKW and EVRG lines on the portfolio page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: BRKW shows a loss with an explicit - sign on both its dollar and percent figures while EVRG shows a gain with a +, and each line displays its percent of the whole portfolio.

ui_instruct.task: Check EVRG's price on the watchlist page, then open the portfolio and look at EVRG's market value.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The market value is $2,684.00 - exactly 40 shares times the $67.10 the watchlist shows - so portfolio values are marked to the watchlist's prices.

ui_instruct.task: Open the alerts area and look at the triggered section.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Exactly one rule shows as triggered - GLCR above $75.00; the DUNE below $34.60 rule is NOT triggered because DUNE sits exactly at $34.60 and above/below are strictly past the line, so a build using at-or-below would wrongly show two.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Five features shipped in quick succession left five different-looking tools; a single visual identity is what a maturing product owes users before more surfaces are added.
follow_ups.instruction: The app has grown into five different-looking tools - time for one identity across the report generator, watchlist, calculator, alerts, and portfolio pages. Everywhere: primary action buttons in navy with white text and fully rounded pill corners; each page's main heading left-aligned with a short gold underline bar beneath it; content cards white with a light gray border and 12px rounded corners; every gain shown as a green filled pill badge and every loss as a red filled pill badge instead of plain colored text; and numeric columns right-aligned in every table. All five pages - if even one keeps the old look it defeats the point.

ui_instruct.task: Open the watchlist page and look at the main heading and the daily change values.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The heading is left-aligned with a short gold underline bar beneath it, and every positive change is a green filled pill badge while every negative change is a red filled pill badge - no plain colored text.

ui_instruct.task: Visit the position size calculator page and then the alerts page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Both pages show the same visual language: navy pill-shaped primary action buttons with white text, left-aligned headings with the gold underline bar, and white content cards with light gray borders and rounded corners - neither page keeps the old look.

ui_instruct.task: Open the restyled portfolio page and read the BRKW line.
ui_instruct.expected_result: BRKW's loss appears as a red filled pill badge reading -$190.00 and -6.1% - the percent computed against its $3,100.00 cost basis, so a build that divides the loss by the $2,910.00 market value and badges -6.5% is wrong - and the table's numeric columns (shares, costs, values, percents) are right-aligned.

ui_instruct.task: On the restyled alerts page, click delete on the ATLS above $150.00 rule, then cancel.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A confirmation is still requested before deletion even after the redesign, and canceling leaves the rule in place.

ui_instruct.task: Open the portfolio page and look at the ATLS line.
ui_instruct.expected_result: There is one consolidated ATLS row (not two separate lots) showing 30 shares at an average cost of $130.00 - the share-weighted figure, not the $135.00 a naive average of the two buy prices gives - with market value $4,275.00.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: As the watchlist grows past a screenful, eyeballing rows stops working; a multi-criteria screener over the same universe is how these users find candidates.
follow_ups.instruction: My watchlist is going to get big, so build me a screener view over it: a sector picker, a max P/E box, and a minimum dividend yield box - typed numbers - and a stock has to pass every filter I've filled in, with blank filters simply not applying and 'max' and 'minimum' including the boundary value itself. Show the matching stocks with a live match count that moves the moment I change any filter, and when nothing qualifies give me a friendly empty message rather than a blank page. It should always screen whatever the watchlist holds at that moment - if I drop a stock from the watchlist, it disappears from screening too.

ui_instruct.task: On the screener, type 16 in the max P/E box and 3.0 in the minimum dividend yield box, leaving the sector unset.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Exactly BRKW, EVRG, and FLNT match and the match count reads 3 - DUNE is excluded because its 2.8% yield fails the minimum even though its P/E 15.3 passes, so the filters combine with AND, not OR.

ui_instruct.task: Clear the other filters, type 4.1 in the minimum dividend yield box, then change it to 4.2.
ui_instruct.expected_result: At 4.1 BRKW is among the matches (its yield equals the boundary and the minimum is inclusive); at 4.2 BRKW drops out of the results.

ui_instruct.task: Pick the Technology sector and type 10 in the max P/E box.
ui_instruct.expected_result: No stocks match, and a friendly empty-state message appears instead of a blank area or an error.

ui_instruct.task: On the watchlist, delete DUNE (accepting the confirmation), then open the screener and type 16 in the max P/E box with no other filters.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The matches are BRKW, EVRG, and FLNT - DUNE no longer appears in screening because it left the watchlist, showing the screener works off the live watchlist.

ui_instruct.task: Click the group-by-sector toggle on the watchlist.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The list regroups by sector with the Technology group containing exactly ATLS and CMET and each of the other five stocks under its own sector; clicking the toggle again restores the single change-sorted list.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Once P/L is visible, drifted allocations are the next pain; a target-weight workbench that prices each holding's dollar drift and skips trades already inside tolerance turns the portfolio's numbers into a concrete trade plan.
follow_ups.instruction: Put a rebalancing workbench next to my portfolio: it lists my holdings with their current weights, and I type a target percent for each - everything reacting live as I type, no submit step. The moment a row has a target, show the dollar amount to buy or sell to bring it there at the current total value - but if a holding already sits within one percentage point of its target, don't prescribe a pointless trade, just flag it as on target. Keep a running unallocated readout showing how far my typed targets are from 100, and give each row an auto-fill that tops its target up with whatever's unallocated so I never do that arithmetic myself. At 40 ATLS / 30 BRKW / 30 EVRG I'd expect sell $327.40 of ATLS, buy $276.70 of EVRG, and BRKW flagged on target - it's only half a point off, and I don't need a $50.70 trade.

ui_instruct.task: In the rebalancing workbench, type targets of 40 for ATLS, 30 for BRKW, and 30 for EVRG.
ui_instruct.expected_result: ATLS reads sell $327.40 and EVRG reads buy $276.70, while BRKW is flagged on target with no trade prescribed - it sits only 0.5 percentage points from its 30% target, inside the one-point tolerance, so a build without the tolerance band that tells the user to buy $50.70 of BRKW is wrong.

ui_instruct.task: Type 40 into ATLS's target and 30 into BRKW's while watching the unallocated readout, then click the auto-fill on the EVRG row.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The unallocated readout moves with every keystroke and reads 30.0 once the two targets are in - ATLS already showing its sell $327.40 move with no submit step - and the auto-fill sets EVRG's target to 30, drops unallocated to 0.0, and EVRG shows its buy $276.70 move.

ui_instruct.task: Before typing any targets, read the current weights shown next to the holdings.
ui_instruct.expected_result: They read ATLS 43.3%, BRKW 29.5%, EVRG 27.2% - matching the portfolio page's allocation and summing to 100.0 - and the page is not blank or erroring on first load.

ui_instruct.task: Open the portfolio page and note the totals row, then open the rebalancing workbench.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The workbench lists exactly the three holdings from the portfolio (ATLS, BRKW, EVRG) and works off the same $9,869.00 total value - no missing or extra positions.

ui_instruct.task: Visit the position size calculator page and then the alerts page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Both pages show the same visual language: navy pill-shaped primary action buttons with white text, left-aligned headings with the gold underline bar, and white content cards with light gray borders and rounded corners - neither page keeps the old look.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: With movers, alerts, and P/L living on separate pages, the pre-open ritual means five clicks; a one-screen briefing that reconciles them all is the power-user payoff.
follow_ups.instruction: Now tie it all together: a morning briefing page I can skim before the open. It pulls today's top gainer and top loser from the watchlist, which of my price alerts have triggered, and my portfolio's total value and overall gain - exactly the numbers those pages show, no drift - and underneath, the whole briefing repeated as a plain-text block sitting right on the page so I can copy it for my group chat. One screen, nothing to click through.

ui_instruct.task: Open the morning briefing and read the top gainer and top loser.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Top gainer is ATLS at +2.4% - not CMET, which ties at +2.4% but loses the alphabetical tiebreak - and top loser is BRKW at -1.2%, not FLNT.

ui_instruct.task: Read the briefing's alerts line and portfolio line.
ui_instruct.expected_result: It reports the GLCR above $75.00 rule as the one triggered alert, and the portfolio at $9,869.00 total value with +$449.00 overall gain - identical to what the alerts and portfolio pages show.

ui_instruct.task: Scroll to the plain-text block at the bottom of the briefing.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A copyable text version of the briefing sits directly on the page and repeats the same facts as the sections above it - ATLS as top gainer, the triggered GLCR alert, the $9,869.00 total - with no download involved and no mismatch.

ui_instruct.task: In the alerts area, add a rule for EVRG, below, with target 70.00, then return to the briefing.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The briefing's triggered alerts now include the new EVRG rule alongside GLCR, since EVRG's $67.10 is strictly below $70.00.

ui_instruct.task: Clear the other filters, type 4.1 in the minimum dividend yield box, then change it to 4.2.
ui_instruct.expected_result: At 4.1 BRKW is among the matches (its yield equals the boundary and the minimum is inclusive); at 4.2 BRKW drops out of the results.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Generated reports currently vanish on navigation; a titled library with a draft-review-final pipeline turns one-off output into a curated research archive.
follow_ups.instruction: Last big push: reports evaporate the second I navigate away, so build me a report library. After generating a report I save it under a title - non-empty and unique, complain otherwise - and it lands in the library as a Draft with a status badge; opening a saved report gives a review step where I have to tick a 'reviewed' box before the Mark Final action will work, and the library lets me filter Drafts from Finals. Preload two so it isn't empty: 'ATLS Q3 Deep Dive' still a Draft, and 'EVRG Income Review' already marked Final.

ui_instruct.task: In the report library, apply the Final filter, then switch to the Draft filter.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The Final view lists exactly one report - 'EVRG Income Review' - and the Draft view exactly one - 'ATLS Q3 Deep Dive' - each carrying its status badge; a build that preloads both reports as Drafts, or shows both under every filter, gets the membership wrong.

ui_instruct.task: In the report library, open 'ATLS Q3 Deep Dive' and try to mark it Final before ticking the reviewed box, then tick the box and mark it Final.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The first attempt is blocked or disabled; after ticking the reviewed confirmation the action works, and back in the library that report's badge now reads Final instead of Draft.

ui_instruct.task: Generate a report for any stock, then try to save it first with an empty title and then with the title 'ATLS Q3 Deep Dive'.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Both saves are rejected - the empty title with a complaint that a title is required, the second with a duplicate-title complaint - and the library still holds exactly one report named 'ATLS Q3 Deep Dive'.

ui_instruct.task: In the report generator, look up GLCR and generate its report, then save it under the title 'GLCR Checkup'.
ui_instruct.expected_result: It appears in the library as a Draft with a Draft badge, alongside the two preloaded reports.

ui_instruct.task: Read the totals row on the portfolio page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Total market value is $9,869.00 and overall gain is +$449.00, with the overall percent shown to one decimal as +4.8%.

target_app_summary: What began as a one-shot stock report generator has grown into a full retail-investor research desk. A seeded watchlist hub became the app's data spine, feeding a strictly-evaluated price alerts center, a live multi-criteria screener, and a lot-level portfolio marked to watchlist prices; on the tool side, a keystroke-live position size calculator and a drift-tolerant rebalancing workbench turn those numbers into trades. A morning briefing reconciles movers, triggered alerts, and portfolio totals onto one copyable screen, and a report library adds a draft-review-final pipeline over the original generator, all unified under a navy-and-gold visual identity. The feature graph is hub-and-spoke around the watchlist (five consumers) with a deep chain running base app -> watchlist -> portfolio -> rebalancer/briefing, so early breakage compounds hard.

edges.what: row buttons prefill the report generator
picks watchlist stocks, evaluates their prices
marks lots to watchlist prices
restyles report generator page
restyles watchlist page
restyles calculator page
restyles alerts pages
restyles portfolio page
screens the live watchlist universe
holdings, weights, and total value
top gainer/loser rollup
triggered alerts rollup
portfolio totals

global_rules.rule: Dollar amounts always display with a $ sign and exactly two decimals; percentages with one decimal and an explicit + or - sign.
Whenever two stocks tie on any number in any ordering or ranking, the tie breaks alphabetically by ticker.
Anything deletable anywhere in the app asks for confirmation before it is actually removed.

instruction: Please implement a sports analytics website that provides basketball betting data and analysis. The website should have functionalities for data visualization, match prediction, and betting recommendations. Users should be able to browse data for basketball, view match history, team rankings, player performance, and make informed betting decisions based on the analysis results. Define the background as ghost white and components as slate gray.

ui_instruct.task: Navigate to the sports data visualization section for basketball.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The page displays graphical representations of sports data relevant to the basketball, such as charts or graphs, without any layout issues or missing data points.

ui_instruct.task: Access the match prediction feature for an upcoming game.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The match prediction page correctly shows predicted outcomes with percentage probabilities, based on current data and analysis, without any technical errors or missing information.

ui_instruct.task: Use the search function to find a specific team's historical match data.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The search results page displays a list of matches involving the specified team, sorted chronologically, with complete match details such as scores and dates.

ui_instruct.task: Check the team rankings page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The page lists teams ranked according to their current standings, with clear markers indicating any ties, and contains accurate data consistent with known league standings.

ui_instruct.task: Evaluate the player performance section for individual stats.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The section shows detailed statistics for players, including metrics like goals, assists, and average ratings, with data clearly labeled and easy to interpret.

ui_instruct.task: Assess the betting recommendations provided for a specific match.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The recommendations offer actionable betting advice backed by data analysis, including relevant statistics or trends that support the suggestions.

ui_instruct.task: Verify that the website uses 'ghost white' as the background color and 'slate gray' as the component color, as specified in the design requirements.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website has a background color of 'ghost white' and components (such as buttons, cards, headers, etc.) are styled with the color 'slate gray', accurately reflecting the design instruction.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Bettors on the site constantly combine legs into parlays and currently do the multiplication on a phone calculator; a live odds-composition tool is the obvious first workbench addition.
follow_ups.instruction: The site's great for browsing stats, but I keep doing parlay math on my phone. Give me a parlay builder page where I stack up legs by typing the American odds for each one plus one total stake, and it shows the combined odds, total payout, and implied probability updating as I type — no calculate button. If a leg isn't a real American line (anything between -99 and +99, like 50), flag it right on that leg and leave it out of the math until it's fixed, don't just zero everything. And two things I want everywhere in this app, now and for anything we build later: money always shows a dollar sign with exactly two decimals, and American odds always carry their sign, like +150 or -110.

ui_instruct.task: On the parlay builder, add two legs by typing -110 for each and type 100 as the stake.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The builder shows a total payout of $364.46 for the $100 stake (odds combined multiplicatively, not added), and the figures appear as you type without pressing any calculate button.

ui_instruct.task: Add two legs, typing -110 in one and 50 in the other, with 100 as the stake.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The 50 leg is visibly flagged as invalid and excluded from the math: the payout reads $190.91, reflecting only the -110 leg.

ui_instruct.task: Clear the legs, add a single leg of +150, and type 100 as the stake.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The payout reads $250.00 and the implied probability reads 40% (or 40.0%).

ui_instruct.task: With that single +150 leg and 100 stake still entered, look at how the money figures are written on the parlay page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Every money figure carries a dollar sign and exactly two decimals (e.g. $250.00, never 250 or $250.0), and the odds display with their sign as +150.

ui_instruct.task: Navigate to the team rankings section of the site.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A rankings view displays multiple basketball teams listed with associated ranking data.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Serious bettors need to track their real bets against their bankroll — the journal becomes the system of record every later analysis feature stands on.
follow_ups.instruction: I want to start logging my actual bets — build me a bet journal. A form to log one (pick the team from the same team list your rankings use, plus the line I took, the date, American odds, and stake — block a zero or negative stake and any fake odds number the same way the parlay builder does), a list of my bets newest-first by date, and each bet opens up so I can settle it as won or lost later, with a summary strip up top showing my record as wins-losses-pending and my net profit counting settled bets only, winnings figured the normal American-odds way. I'm starting from a $1,000 bankroll. Load exactly these eight to start, I'll add more later: Lakers -4.5 on Mar 3, $100 at -110, won; Bulls +6.5 on Mar 8, $80 at -105, won; Celtics ML on Mar 5, $50 at +140, lost; Warriors ML on Mar 10, $60 at +125, won; Suns +3.5 on Mar 15, $75 at +100, won; Heat -2.5 on Mar 7, $120 at -110, lost; Knicks ML on Mar 18, $100 at +150, still pending; and Nuggets -7.5 on Mar 20, $70 at -120, also pending. One more thing for everywhere in this app going forward: wherever a bet's status shows, make it a little badge — green for won, red for lost, gray for pending.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Once real bets accumulate in the journal, bettors want to know if they're actually winning — win rate, ROI, streaks and per-team profit are the questions they ask first.
follow_ups.instruction: Now that my bets live in the journal, build a performance page that crunches them. I want my win rate and ROI — win rate over settled bets only so the pending ones don't pull it down, ROI as net profit over what I staked on settled bets, both to one decimal — and put the net profit dollar figure itself right on the page next to the ROI so I can see the money behind the percentage. Then my longest winning streak going by game date, not the order the bets got logged, and a profit ranking by team where a tie in profit gets settled alphabetically. It should re-crunch whenever I settle something over in the journal.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Bettors with money already riding want to know if those stakes were sized right — a Kelly checkup that grades the journal's pending bets against the live bankroll turns the tracked data into staking judgment.
follow_ups.instruction: Now that the journal knows what I've got riding, I want a sanity check on my stake sizing. Build me a stake checkup page: it lists my pending bets straight from the journal, I pick one and type in what I reckon the real win probability is, and as I type it shows the Kelly-suggested stake for that bet — figured from the bet's own odds and my current bankroll, the $1,000 I started with plus whatever the journal says I'm up or down on settled bets, with that bankroll figure shown right on the page. Give it a half-Kelly option that halves the Kelly fraction since full Kelly is spicy, and a verdict telling me how many dollars over or under the suggestion my actual stake sits. And if my probability doesn't actually beat the line's break-even, don't show me a negative stake — tell me flat out it's a no-bet at any size.

follow_ups.instruction: Let's plan ahead. From the review queue, committing a plan drops it into the journal as a pending bet and clears it from the queue. Have one waiting for me already: Bulls +3.5 for $50 at -110.

Pending bets stay out of recaps entirely.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: After tracking and staking tools, the natural capstone question is whether the bettor's variable staking beat a boring flat stake — a counterfactual replay of their own journal answers it.
follow_ups.instruction: Been wondering if my stake sizing actually helps. Give me a what-if page that replays every settled bet from my journal at one flat stake — default it to $100, but let me type any amount — and shows the simulated net side by side with my actual net and the difference between them, recomputing as I change the number. It should say how many bets went into the replay, and pending bets stay out of it, obviously. The actual figure should line up with what the performance page says. If I type zero or a negative stake, flag it instead of showing bogus numbers.

target_app_summary: The base basketball-betting analytics site (rankings, match history, player stats, predictions) grows into a full bettor's workbench. It gains an odds-composition parlay builder, then a bet journal with a $1,000 bankroll and settle workflow that becomes the hub of the app: an analytics page aggregates it, a Kelly stake checkup grades its pending bets against the journal bankroll, a planning board commits queued plans into it, a screener cross-references it while filtering the planning slate, a recap composer windows it by date into a shareable archive, and a flat-stake what-if simulator replays it counterfactually. A 'courtside' design restyle unifies five pages late in the ladder. The graph is hub-and-spoke around the journal (R3) with one deep chain R1->R3->R6->R7 and a reconciling capstone (R10 must match R4's figures).

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Homeowners weighing an expansion all ask the same first question — how big a system do I need and when does it pay off — so a live sizing calculator is the natural pre-purchase companion to the monitoring dashboard.
follow_ups.instruction: Love the dashboard. The thing people keep asking me is 'how big a system do I actually need?' — so add a sizing calculator page where I type my monthly electric bill, my rate in $/kWh, average sun hours per day, panel wattage in watts, and installed cost per watt, and it works out my monthly usage, the recommended system size in kW (monthly usage divided by 30 days times sun hours), how many panels that takes (round up — nobody sells 17.8 panels), the upfront cost, and the payback in years to one decimal. It has to recalculate as I type, no calculate button, and if a field is blank or zero just show a gentle nudge instead of NaN soup. One formatting rule for this whole app, now and for anything we add later: energy always reads as kWh with exactly one decimal, like 1200.0 kWh.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Once a property runs more than one array, owners need a fleet view — per-array records, status tracking, and rollups — before any per-array analytics or operations work can exist.
follow_ups.instruction: We've got more than one array on the property now, so give me a fleet registry page — start it with exactly these six and I'll grow it later: South Roof (5.2 kW capacity, 24.7 kWh yesterday, 512.0 kWh so far this month, Healthy), Garage East (3.0 kW, 12.6 kWh, 300.4 kWh, Healthy), Barn West (4.4 kW, 11.0 kWh, 205.0 kWh, Degraded), Carport (2.5 kW, 10.5 kWh, 248.6 kWh, Healthy), Field Ground Mount (6.0 kW, 18.0 kWh, 410.0 kWh, Degraded), and Pool House (2.5 kW, 9.0 kWh, 96.0 kWh, Offline). I want a summary strip up top — total capacity, yesterday's combined output, and how many are Healthy vs Degraded vs Offline — with one wrinkle: an Offline array wasn't actually feeding anything, so its stale yesterday number stays out of the combined output (capacity is nameplate, count that for everyone). Plus a status filter, and when I filter, that summary has to recount over just the arrays I'm looking at, not the whole fleet. Let me change an array's status right from its row. Status colors are a thing now: Healthy gets a green badge, Degraded amber, Offline red — use those everywhere an array shows up in this app from here on. And on the main dashboard, break the live generation readout down by array — an Offline one like Pool House shouldn't show as contributing anything.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: With six arrays in service, things break — owners need a real report-queue-resolve maintenance flow tied to the fleet registry instead of sticky notes.
follow_ups.instruction: Panels break, so let's do maintenance tickets properly: from any array I pick, let me file a ticket with a description (required — don't let me submit a blank one) and a priority of High, Medium, or Low. Open tickets live on a queue page sorted High first, and resolving one moves it over to a separate resolved list. Give the queue a strip up top showing how much fleet capacity is sitting under an open ticket — add up the capacities of the arrays that have at least one open ticket, and an array whose only tickets are resolved stays out of that number. Seed it with two open ones — a Low 'Panel soiling' on Barn West, and a High 'Inverter fault' on Field Ground Mount — plus an already-resolved 'Storm damage' on Pool House. House rule from now on, everywhere in the app: anything that resolves, deletes, or dismisses something asks me to confirm before it happens.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Owners constantly wonder 'can I run the AC and charge the car right now?' — a live load planner that balances appliance draw against the dashboard's current generation answers that in one glance.
follow_ups.instruction: Here's a fun one: a load planner page where I can see what I can run straight off the sun. Don't invent the available power — read it off the fleet: call it every online array producing at 20% of its rated capacity right now, with an Offline one giving nothing (same way the dashboard breakdown treats it), and show that same figure as the dashboard's live generation total so the two never disagree — and print power on this planner, and that dashboard generation total, in kW with exactly two decimals, like 4.22 kW, so a small deficit doesn't get rounded invisible. Give the planner a list of appliances I can flip on and off — EV Charger 7.2 kW, AC 3.5 kW, Heat Pump Dryer 1.4 kW, Pool Pump 1.1 kW — plus a row where I add a custom one by typing a name and its draw in watts (I'll type watts, like 1500, so convert). The meter has to move the instant I toggle or type: show my remaining headroom, make it very obvious when I've tipped into deficit and by exactly how much, and when I'm in the red, point me at the smallest single appliance I could switch off to get back into the black.

ui_instruct.task: Open the load planner with nothing switched on and read its available-power baseline.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The baseline reads 4.22 kW — 20% of the fleet's 21.1 kW of online capacity; a build that let Offline Pool House's 2.5 kW into the baseline shows 4.72 kW instead.

ui_instruct.task: On the load planner, toggle on the AC and the Pool Pump, then read the meter and the shed suggestion.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The meter flips to a clearly-flagged deficit of 0.38 kW (4.60 kW drawn against 4.22 kW available), and the shed suggestion names the Pool Pump — its 1.1 kW is the smallest single switch-off that clears the 0.38 kW gap; a build that just points at the biggest load (the AC) is wrong.

ui_instruct.task: On the load planner with nothing else toggled on, add a custom appliance named 'Space Heater' and type 1500 into its watts field, then watch the meter.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The meter moves as the number is typed and settles at 2.72 kW headroom — the 1500 was converted from watts to 1.50 kW; a build that subtracts it as kilowatts shows an enormous deficit.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The dashboard total and the planner baseline both read 4.22 kW, with Pool House contributing nothing in the breakdown — the planner is anchored to the same fleet-derived reading, not a separate made-up number.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: At month's end owners settle up with the utility; a statement composer that aggregates the fleet's month-to-date output — honoring which arrays actually fed the grid — turns the registry's records into money.
follow_ups.instruction: Bill time — build me a statement page that writes up my month so far as a copyable block of text right on screen: a line for each array with its month-to-date output, then the fleet total, my home consumption (use 1240.5 kWh), the net surplus, and the credit. For pricing, I'm choosing between two utility plans, so let me pick one right on the page — Standard at $0.12/kWh, the default, or Time-of-Use export at $0.20/kWh — and the whole statement should redo itself the moment I switch. One catch the utility is picky about: only arrays that are actually online feed the grid, so anything sitting Offline in the registry — Pool House and its 96.0 kWh, as things stand — stays off the statement entirely, line item and totals both.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: With a fleet, tickets, and a leaderboard in play, owners can't keep eyeballing pages for trouble — user-defined threshold rules that evaluate the same numbers the leaderboard trusts are the natural monitoring layer.
follow_ups.instruction: I can't keep eyeballing the dashboard for trouble — give me an alert center. I define rules like 'metric below threshold' (threshold typed in, strictly below, so equal doesn't fire) over either an array's efficiency — same numbers and same lineup as the leaderboard, so an array that isn't on the board can't raise an efficiency alert — or the battery level from the dashboard, which is sitting at 62% these days, keep it there. Start me off with one rule already saved: efficiency below 4.00. Triggered alerts land in an inbox naming which array or metric tripped which rule — let me dismiss one once I've dealt with it — and the inbox should react right away when I add a rule or when the underlying data changes.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: The fleet keeps growing, and hand-editing new arrays into the registry risks bad data — a guided commissioning flow with validation and a projected-impact review is how a serious fleet tool onboards hardware.

Step one takes the name, capacity in kW, and yesterday's output in kWh, and it shouldn't let me continue with a blank or non-numeric capacity or a name that's already in the registry. Step two is a review screen that shows me the computed efficiency and where the new array would land in the leaderboard rankings before I commit. Confirming drops it into the registry as Healthy, and everything downstream — the summary totals, the board — picks it up. First one to run through it: Workshop Roof, 3.0 kW, 13.5 kWh yesterday.

target_app_summary: The base app was a single-home solar dashboard (live generation/consumption/battery readouts, historical queries, charts). Over nine requests it grows into a full residential solar operations product pulling in several directions: pre-purchase planning (a live sizing/payback calculator), fleet management (a six-array registry with status-aware rollups that also feeds a per-array breakdown into the dashboard's live panel), operations (a maintenance ticket workflow and a rule-based alert center), analytics (an efficiency leaderboard with tie-breaks and offline exclusion), day-to-day usage (a live appliance load planner whose power budget is 20% of the registry's online capacity, with smallest-single-shed suggestions), billing (an on-screen monthly statement composer with selectable tariff plans that honors offline exclusions), plus a full visual restyle and a guided commissioning wizard capstone. The dependency spine runs R1 -> registry (R3) -> leaderboard (R5) -> alert center (R9) / commissioning wizard (R10), with the ticket workflow (R4) feeding leaderboard flags and both the statement (R7) and the load planner (R6) drawing on registry data — so a broken registry or leaderboard poisons four later requests.

edges.what: dashboard's live generation panel, extended with a per-array breakdown
registry arrays (with status badges) tickets are filed against, and their capacities the queue's at-risk strip sums
array capacities, yesterday outputs, and editable statuses it ranks
open High-priority tickets it flags on the board
online-only fleet capacity (Offline arrays excluded) that sets the planner's available-power baseline
dashboard's live generation total the planner's fleet-derived baseline must match
per-array month-to-date output and Offline status it aggregates
dashboard pages it restyles
registry page it restyles
ticket queue and ticket-filing surfaces it restyles
leaderboard page it restyles
leaderboard's efficiency values and Offline-excluded lineup the rules evaluate
dashboard's battery percentage the battery rules watch
registry, rollup, and name-uniqueness the commissioned array lands in
leaderboard ranking the review step projects a position into

global_rules.rule: Every energy figure anywhere in the app is displayed as kWh with exactly one decimal place (e.g. 1200.0 kWh).
Array status is color-badge-coded everywhere an array appears: Healthy = green, Degraded = amber, Offline = red.
Any action that resolves, deletes, or dismisses something — anywhere in the app — asks for confirmation before it happens.

instruction: Please implement a text-based strategy browser game where players can choose a race, manage resources, upgrade, and battle. The game should have multiple pages, including the base page, ranking page, store, train page, workers page, upgrades page, bank page, messages page, and reports page. Players can choose from four races: Humans, Dragonborns, Elves, and Dwarfs, each with unique attributes. Players can manage resources, including gold, iron, wood, and wheat, and can upgrade their city, workers, and soldiers. Design the site using seashell as the background and crimson for content blocks.

ui_instruct.task: Navigate to the "Choose Race" page and select each race (Humans, Dragonborns, Elves, Dwarfs) one by one and back to the homepage after selecting for another select.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Each click on a race should display specific attributes unique to that race, and the selection should be confirmed on the page.

ui_instruct.task: On the base page, attempt to allocate resources (gold, iron, wood, wheat) to upgrade the city.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The resources should be deducted from the total, and an upgrade confirmation message should appear with visible changes to the city level or attributes.

ui_instruct.task: Visit the "Ranking Page" and verify the rank listing of players.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The page should display a sorted list of players by rank, with accurate and clear presentation relevant to their performance metrics.

ui_instruct.task: Go to the "Store" and purchase an item using available resources.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The selected item should be removed from the store and added to your inventory, with the appropriate deduction in resources.

ui_instruct.task: Access the "Train Page" and begin training workers or soldiers.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Training should commence with a status update visible, and there should be an indication of resource consumption related to this activity.

ui_instruct.task: Navigate to the "Workers Page" and assign a task to workers.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The task should be acknowledged by the system with relevant feedback on expected completion, and any resource costs should be visibly deducted.

ui_instruct.task: Visit the "Upgrades Page" and attempt to upgrade a soldier.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The upgrade should succeed, show updated soldier stats, and the necessary resources should be spent.

ui_instruct.task: Access the "Bank Page" and deposit gold.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The deposited gold should reflect in the bank balance, deducting from available on-hand funds with confirmation of the transaction.

ui_instruct.task: Verify that the website uses 'seashell' as the background color and 'crimson' as the component color, as specified in the design requirements.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website has a background color of 'seashell' and components (such as buttons, cards, headers, etc.) are styled with the color 'crimson', accurately reflecting the design instruction.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Players committing armies need to predict outcomes before risking troops - a war-room odds calculator is the first tool a strategy player asks for, and its power math becomes the backbone of later raid planning.
follow_ups.instruction: Before I commit my armies anywhere I want a war room page with a battle odds calculator. I type how many swordsmen, archers, and cavalry I'm sending - 10 power per swordsman, 6 per archer, 15 per cavalry - pick a race, and the total attack power updates live with every keystroke: Dragonborns get +20%, Dwarfs +15%, Elves +10%, Humans +5%, always dropped down to a whole number. There's also a field for the enemy's defense power, and it should call it plainly - victory likely when my power's higher, defeat likely when it's lower, and even odds on an exact tie. Blank fields just mean zero, no errors. One thing for the whole app while you're in there, now and for anything we build later: any number in the thousands gets comma separators, like 12,500.

ui_instruct.task: On the war room battle odds calculator, type 3 into the swordsmen field and 1 into the cavalry field, and choose Elves as the race.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The attack power reads 49 - the 10% Elf bonus on 45 base power is rounded down to a whole number, not shown as 49.5 or 50.

ui_instruct.task: In the battle odds calculator, type 10 into swordsmen, choose Humans, and type 105 into the enemy defense power field.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The verdict shows the even/tie outcome (attack power 105 equals defense 105), not victory or defeat.

ui_instruct.task: In the battle odds calculator, type 100 into swordsmen with Dragonborns chosen, then change it to 200.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The attack power updates immediately as typed with no submit step - reading 1,200 and then 2,400.

ui_instruct.task: In the battle odds calculator, type 1000 into the swordsmen field with Humans chosen.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The attack power displays as 10,500 with a comma thousands separator, per the app-wide number format.

ui_instruct.task: From the base page, use the site's navigation to open the ranking page, the bank page, and the reports page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Each of the three pages opens with its own content - none of them is missing or blank.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: As players outgrow their own city the game needs opponents with real stats - a scouting ledger turns rivals into actionable intelligence with a threat ranking that raw power alone gets wrong.
follow_ups.instruction: My scouts came back - I need a Scouting Ledger page for rival kingdoms. Load it with exactly these seven, I'll add more later: Ironhold (Dwarfs, army power 9000, gold reserves 4200, 6 leagues out, hostile), Sunspire (Elves, 8400 power, 7500 gold, 4 leagues, neutral), Grimfang (Dragonborns, 12000 power, 3000 gold, 10 leagues, hostile), Willowmere (Humans, 3600 power, 9800 gold, 3 leagues, friendly), Emberfall (Dragonborns, 7200 power, 5100 gold, 6 leagues, hostile), Thornwall (Humans, 5500 power, 2750 gold, 5 leagues, neutral), and Frostpeak (Dwarfs, 6000 power, 6600 gold, 4 leagues, hostile). Rank them by threat - army power divided by leagues of distance, whole numbers - highest first, and when two tie, alphabetical order settles it. Give me a way to filter down to a single stance, keeping that same threat order in whatever's left. And a rule for everywhere in this app from now on: stances always get colored badges - crimson for hostile, goldenrod for neutral, seagreen for friendly.

ui_instruct.task: Open the Scouting Ledger page and read the top three kingdoms in the threat ranking.

ui_instruct.expected_result: Exactly four kingdoms remain - Frostpeak, Ironhold, Emberfall, Grimfang in that threat order - and Sunspire, Thornwall, and Willowmere are hidden.

ui_instruct.task: On the Scouting Ledger, look at the stance badges on Willowmere's and Thornwall's rows.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Willowmere shows a seagreen friendly badge and Thornwall a goldenrod neutral badge (hostile rows like Grimfang use crimson).

ui_instruct.task: On the Scouting Ledger, read Grimfang's army power and Willowmere's gold reserves.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Both display with comma separators - 12,000 and 9,800 - matching the app-wide number format.

ui_instruct.task: On the war room battle odds calculator, type 3 into the swordsmen field and 1 into the cavalry field, and choose Elves as the race.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The attack power reads 49 - the 10% Elf bonus on 45 base power is rounded down to a whole number, not shown as 49.5 or 50.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: With intel and odds math in hand, the player's next job is actually striking - a guided raid flow converts the scouting ledger and calculator into launched battles that land on the reports page.
follow_ups.instruction: Time to hit back. Build a raid planner that walks me through it: pick a target - only the hostile kingdoms from my scouting ledger should be offered - then assign swordsmen, archers, and cavalry, then a review screen that shows my raid power using the same unit math and race bonus as the battle odds calculator, plus estimated loot of 30% of the target's gold reserves rounded down. And in my realm the estimate is never wrong: a launched raid always brings home exactly that figure, and the ledger's scouted reserves never drain - hit the same kingdom twice and you loot the same amount both times. No launching with zero troops assigned. When it goes, a raid entry lands on the reports page saying who I hit and the loot taken - that same 30% figure - and backfill my reports with four past raids while you're at it: Grimfang for 900 gold, Ironhold for 1,260, Emberfall for 1,530, and Grimfang again for the same 900 - identical haul both times, exactly like the rule says. Also, app-wide from here on out, forever: anything that commits me - launching a raid, whatever we add later - asks are-you-sure before it happens.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The raid cannot go out with zero troops - however the planner enforces it (a blocked launch or an unusable launch control), nothing launches and no new report entry is created.

ui_instruct.expected_result: A new raid report against Grimfang appears alongside the four backfilled raids, showing the loot taken.

ui_instruct.task: Open the Scouting Ledger page and read the top three kingdoms in the threat ranking.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Sunspire is first (threat 2,100), Frostpeak second and Ironhold third (both 1,500, alphabetical tiebreak) - Grimfang is NOT on top despite having the highest raw army power.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Resource-management players always end up lopsided on iron or wheat - a caravan exchange gives the economy a sink that commits real transactions into a ledger and the bank, with a per-deal haul limit and fee math that punishes sloppy rounding.
follow_ups.instruction: The treasury needs love - give me a Merchant Exchange page where I strike deals with the traveling caravan, one resource per deal: I pick what I'm selling - iron fetches 3 gold apiece, wood 2, wheat 1 - type how much, and the merchant's quote redraws with every keystroke: gross gold, his 5% fee always rounded up to the next whole coin, and what I actually pocket. He won't haul more than 250 units in a single deal - ask for more and the sale is refused with the reason spelled out. Completing a sale appends it to a trade ledger right on the page and bumps the gold on my bank page by the net amount. Start the ledger with two deals I already made: 200 iron that netted 570 gold, and 120 wheat that netted 114.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: A single renown score gives players their long-term standing across war, diplomacy, and questing - and a threshold-based title ladder turns that score into a metagame progression system that must recompute the title and next-rank countdown live, which a static or unrounded build gets visibly wrong.
follow_ups.instruction: Put a Renown panel on the ranking page that scores my whole reign. Renown is all the gold ever looted in raids divided by 100 and dropped to a whole number, plus 50 for every sealed treaty, plus 25 for every quest reward I've claimed - show those three lines and the grand total. And renown earns titles: under 100 renown I'm a mere Squire, 100 makes me a Knight, 250 a Baron, 500 a Warlord - the panel names my current title and says exactly how much more renown reaches the next rank, and a Warlord just gets told there's no rank higher. It all has to move the instant anything changes - I claim a quest or seal a treaty, and the title, the countdown, and every line are already right when I come back to the ranking page.

ui_instruct.task: Open the ranking page and read the Renown panel in full.

follow_ups.instruction: The realm deserves a grander look - roll out our Age of Ashes style across the scouting ledger, merchant exchange, diplomacy hall, quest board, and the original base, bank, and reports pages. Content blocks go from crimson to deep maroon with visibly rounded corners, every page's main heading is centered and starts with a small crossed-swords mark, primary action buttons - complete sale, seal treaty, claim reward, all of them - turn dark goldenrod with white text, and stance badges become fully rounded pills while keeping their exact colors. target_app_summary: The base text-strategy game (city, four resources, four races, ranking/store/train/bank/reports pages) grows into a full campaign sandbox. A war-room battle odds calculator feeds a guided raid-planning workflow that writes entries to the reports page; a seeded scouting ledger of seven rival kingdoms supplies threat rankings, stances, and raid targets; a diplomacy hall lets neutral rivals be bought into friendship; and a merchant exchange converts surplus resources into bank gold. On top of these sit three derived layers - a war dossier aggregating raid history per rival with tie-aware rankings, a quest board that pays out on trading/treaty/raiding milestones already on record, and a renown panel on the ranking page compounding loot, treaties, and claimed quests into a Squire-to-Warlord title ladder with a live next-rank countdown - before a final Age of Ashes restyle unifies old and new pages. The feature graph has two deep chains (calculator -> raid planner -> dossier; ledger -> diplomacy -> quest board -> prestige) plus a hub at the raid planner feeding three later consumers.

Show a running total of the debt carried by whatever leads are currently visible - when I filter, that total should follow the filter. follow_ups.feature_rationale: Staff pull raw tradeline dumps from bureau reports and re-type them by hand; a paste-in reader that parses lines into a flagged accounts table live turns an hour of drudgery into seconds.
follow_ups.instruction: My assistants burn hours re-typing the raw tradeline dumps we pull out of bureau reports. Give the staff side a report reader page: one big box where I paste an export, one account per line, in the shape Creditor | balance | limit | status (status is open or closed). As I type or paste, a results table should rebuild itself instantly - no parse button - showing each account's creditor, balance, limit, and utilization as a whole-number percent of its limit, with a 'High' flag on any open account sitting above 30% utilization. Closed accounts never get the flag no matter how maxed out they are, and exactly 30% doesn't count as above. A line that doesn't break into those four parts shouldn't wreck the table - drop it into a 'couldn't read' list underneath, skip blank lines quietly, and keep a running count of accounts read versus lines skipped.

target_app_summary: The base lead-gen site for a credit repair company grows into a full front-office suite for the firm. On the operations side it gains a leads pipeline that captures every site-form submission, a multi-step enrollment flow that converts leads into paying clients on fixed plans, a consultation scheduler with a double-booking-proof slot grid, and a client progress hub that ranks active cases by dispute-letter volume with a debt tiebreak. On the tooling side staff get a live dispute letter builder with validation and a saved-letter library, a tradeline report reader that parses raw bureau paste-ins into a live flagged-utilization table, and a quote builder with a 3-service bundle-discount boundary. A brand restyle unifies four surfaces, and a success-stories publisher closes the loop by pulling verified stats from the progress hub onto the public site. The graph runs a 4-deep chain (form -> pipeline -> enrollment -> progress hub -> success stories) plus scheduler and letter-builder branches off the pipeline.

letter builder picks which pipeline lead a letter is for
enrollment converts a pipeline lead and flips its status to Enrolled

restyles the public home/services pages
restyles the leads pipeline
restyles the dispute letter builder
restyles the client progress hub
scheduler books pipeline leads; booking flips New leads to Contacted
stories are publishable only for enrolled clients
story auto-fills plan, band, and letter count from the progress hub

global_rules.rule: Every dollar amount app-wide is shown as whole dollars with a $ sign and thousands comma (e.g. $12,400), no cents.
Every credit score shown anywhere gets a colored band badge: red 'Poor' under 580, amber 'Fair' 580-669, green 'Good' 670 and up.
Anywhere the app keeps a list of saved things (libraries, published items), the newest saved entry sits on top.

target_app_summary: What began as a four-page brochure site for a clinical office has grown into a full patient-facing practice portal. Discovery grew first: a filterable, rating-sorted provider directory of the office's seven clinicians, later joined by a side-by-side doctor comparison tool with a computed value score. A cost dimension grew next: a live visit cost estimator with add-ons and insurance math, and eventually an on-screen billing statement generator; alongside them, a self-service screening schedule checker turns age and risk factors into a due-now-versus-upcoming plan with rule-based age thresholds. The operational spine is the appointment request workflow (form, review, My Requests list with status pills), which feeds a practice dashboard of per-doctor rollups and pending revenue, and gains a specialty-based visit-prep checklist flow whose Ready state gates what the billing statement may include. A mid-life visual refresh replaced the original cyan look with a white-card, deep-teal design system across all major pages. The feature graph has a deep operational chain (directory -> requests -> prep -> billing) with the dashboard and estimator hanging off the directory, and two standalone-ish tools (screening check, comparison) plus the restyle fanning in from five earlier surfaces.

target_app_summary: What began as a one-page cornsilk-and-peru promo site for Fundraiser Day has grown into a full event-operations product for the organizing committee. It gained a Team Fundraising Board with live progress tracking, a donor-facing Pledge Calculator, a Volunteer Shifts signup workflow with capacity management, and an Event Analytics rollup over teams and staffing. A Donation Desk feeds cash-and-check entries into the board's totals; that ledger in turn powers a tiered Donor Wall, and a Sponsor Us card composer lets businesses preview and inject their offers back into the original homepage carousel. A design pass unifies the visual language across all pages, and a Report Builder compiles teams, staffing, and donor recognition into a copyable wrap-up. The graph fans out from the pinned team seed (board -> analytics, shifts, desk) and runs one deep chain: board -> donation desk -> donor wall -> wrap-up report.

target_app_summary: The base site was a simple house-cleaning service page with booking, inquiry, status check, and contact info. Over nine milestones it grows into a full customer platform: a live instant-quote calculator that feeds the booking flow, a pinned eight-record service history with rollups and a tie-broken cleaner leaderboard, a recurring-plan wizard that reuses the quote engine's pricing, a screenable cleaner directory whose cards count completed jobs from the history, a validated issue-reporting workflow against completed jobs, a loyalty program with multiplier-based points and validated redemption, a room-by-room checklist builder that attaches to the plan or the scheduled booking, a monthly budget planner that judges each month's completed spend and the active plan's projected cost against a customer-set cap, and a full visual refresh across all major surfaces. The graph centers on two hubs: the R3 history seed (consumed by the directory, issues, loyalty, checklists, and the budget planner) and the R2 pricing engine (consumed by the plan wizard, which in turn feeds checklists and the budget planner), giving a R1->R2->R4->R8 chain three deep.

target_app_summary: A year on, The All-In Bourbon Bar's site has grown from a brochure into the bar's full digital front-of-house. Discovery grew a screener-equipped bourbon library and a personal tasting journal whose ratings flow back onto the shelf; tooling grew a live flight builder and a keystroke-live proofing bench that does the dilution algebra; operations grew a session-aware poker seat map with membership validation and capacity-tracked event RSVPs with waitlists. A Rail Club rewards ledger sits on top, computing points live from claimed poker seats and journal tastings, and a Plan My Night wizard composes saved flights, event seats, and poker seat claims into one costed, points-previewed itinerary. A Midnight Rail restyle unifies the look across the home/menu, library, builder, and rewards surfaces. The graph runs deep: library -> journal -> rewards -> night planner is a four-level chain, with the planner also standing on the seat map and RSVP flows.

target_app_summary: A year on, the lead CRM has grown from a simple list-and-message tool into a full revenue workbench. Discovery grew a multi-criteria lead screener with saved presets; messaging grew a merge-field Template Studio; execution grew a template-driven Follow-up Queue; and analytics grew three layers deep: a rule-based Score Leaderboard, a Monday Digest that reconciles pipeline, tiers, and open follow-ups, and a Forecast Commit Board that turns score tiers into a weighted forecast reps work deal by deal, committing or benching leads from the board or straight from the leaderboard. Data hygiene arrived as a Dedupe & Merge Center that must keep the screener and digest honest after merges, reps got a tiered Commission Calculator wired to lead records, and a brand restyle unified five surfaces. The feature graph has one deep spine (base leads -> templates -> follow-ups -> digest -> dedupe reconciliation) plus a scoring branch feeding both the digest and the forecast.

target_app_summary: What began as a simple technical-articles-and-solutions site grows into a full engineering knowledge platform. A pinned seven-article library feeds an Insights dashboard (rollups, category view-shares, tie-broken top-rated spotlight), a per-author Contributors leaderboard with a points formula, a click-driven guided troubleshooter, curated learning paths with completion math, and a Library Health audit with flag-based scoring. Alongside the data spine sit a standalone Capacity Planner calculator, a solution-proposal review pipeline (draft -> pending queue -> approve/reject) whose published solutions feed both the leaderboard and the health audit, a weekly Digest composer that embeds dashboard and leaderboard numbers into a copyable on-screen roundup, and a blueprint-style visual identity applied across four pages. The graph's deepest chain runs base app -> seeded library/dashboard -> proposal pipeline -> leaderboard -> digest, so early breakage compounds through the late requests.

instruction: Please implement an anonymous campus discussion platform for students to communicate and discuss. The platform should have a discussion forum feature that allows students to anonymously post, reply to posts, and participate in discussions. Students should be able to browse and search posts, follow topics of interest, and receive notifications. The platform should ensure user privacy and security, protecting students' personal information. Configure your theme with honeydew as background and dark olive green as component color.

ui_instruct.task: Post an anonymous message in the discussion forum.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The message appears in the forum without displaying any personal information about the sender.

ui_instruct.task: Reply anonymously to an existing post in the discussion forum.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The reply is successfully added and visible under the original post, maintaining the anonymity of the responder.

ui_instruct.task: Search for a post using a specific keyword such as math.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The search results display relevant posts containing the keyword entered, and irrelevant posts are not shown.

ui_instruct.task: Follow a topic of interest.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The user interface indicates that the topic is being followed, and related notifications are received if this is part of the system design.

ui_instruct.task: Navigate through different topics and the home page without errors or dead ends.
ui_instruct.expected_result: All navigation actions direct the user to the intended pages without loading errors or broken links.

ui_instruct.task: Test the notification feature by simulating a new post in a followed topic.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The user receives a notification about the new post without revealing any user's personal details.

ui_instruct.task: Verify that the website uses 'honeydew' as the background color and 'dark olive green' as the component color, as specified in the design requirements.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website has a background color of 'honeydew' and components (such as buttons, cards, headers, etc.) are styled with the color 'dark olive green', accurately reflecting the design instruction.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Browsing a growing forum, students need a topic-level read on where campus conversation actually is, not just a raw post list.
follow_ups.instruction: The forum needs a pulse-check page — call it Campus Pulse — where every topic rolls up into an entry showing how many posts it has, its combined upvotes, and its single most-upvoted post, ranked biggest combined tally first, plus a toggle that re-ranks using only the recent stuff from Weeks 3 and 4. Seed the forum with exactly these eight posts so there's something to chew on, each tagged with the week it went up: 'Midterm survival guide' (Exams, 67 upvotes, 20 replies, Week 2), 'Quiet hours petition' (Dorm Life, 42, 12, Week 1), 'Best ramen hacks' (Cafeteria, 42, 5, Week 3), 'Radiator rattling in Hall B' (Dorm Life, 8, 3, Week 3), 'Study buddy for Stats 201' (Exams, 15, 9, Week 4), 'Chess club open night' (Clubs, 21, 4, Week 4), 'Meal plan swap thread' (Cafeteria, 33, 14, Week 4), 'Late-night library noise' (Dorm Life, 15, 6, Week 2) — exactly these, I'll add more myself. And two habits I want baked in everywhere in this app, now and for anything we build later: upvote tallies always wear a little caret, like ^42, and any list or tally with nothing to show says 'All quiet for now' instead of sitting blank.

ui_instruct.task: Open the Campus Pulse page in its default whole-semester view and read the topic ranking.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The topics run Exams, Cafeteria, Dorm Life, Clubs from top to bottom, with Exams showing a combined tally of ^82.

ui_instruct.task: On Campus Pulse, switch to the recent (Weeks 3 and 4) view.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Cafeteria ranks first with ^75 and Dorm Life falls to last with ^8 — a different order from the whole-semester Exams-first ranking.

ui_instruct.task: Find the Dorm Life entry on Campus Pulse in the whole-semester view.
ui_instruct.expected_result: It shows a combined tally of ^65 and names 'Quiet hours petition' as the topic's top post.

ui_instruct.task: In the forum, publish a new anonymous post in the Clubs topic titled 'Frisbee pickup?', then open Campus Pulse in the whole-semester view.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Clubs now counts 2 posts while its combined tally stays ^21 and its top post remains 'Chess club open night'.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The reply appears under the post with no real name or identity attached to it.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Half the threads are 'which option?' questions; structured polls with live-validated creation settle them faster than reply-counting.
follow_ups.instruction: Students keep asking pick-one questions, so give us a Poll Studio: a page where anyone can spin up a poll with a question and 2 to 5 answer options, with a live ballot preview that redraws on every keystroke and refuses to create while two options are the same thing (even 'Gym' versus 'gym') or fewer than two are filled in — and don't just quietly block it, say what's wrong in words the instant the problem appears in the text, and clear the message the instant it's fixed. Results list options most-voted first with each share shown to one decimal, like 43.8%, updating the instant a vote lands — and a poll nobody has voted on yet counts as having nothing to show. By the way, anywhere in this whole app that sorts things by a number, break ties alphabetically — now and forever. Start it off with one poll already running, 'Best late-night study spot', with Library at 7 votes, Student Union at 5, and Dorm lounge at 4.

ui_instruct.expected_result: Cafeteria ranks first with ^75 and Dorm Life falls to last with ^8 — a different order from the whole-semester Exams-first ranking.

follow_ups.instruction: People keep telling me about junk posts in person, which is silly. follow_ups.feature_rationale: The owner hand-writes weekly recaps for class group chats, and what readers actually ask is what's heating up or dying down; a computed momentum digest automates that.
follow_ups.instruction: Every Friday I paste a recap into the class group chats, and the question people actually ask is 'what's heating up?'. So build me a Week in Review page: I pick a week (2, 3, or 4) and every topic gets one line comparing that week's combined upvotes against the week before — label each line climbing, cooling, or steady, show the size of the swing as a tally, and order the lines biggest climb first down to biggest drop; a topic that didn't move just reads steady, no number needed, and every topic keeps its line even across a pair of quiet weeks. Tack the current standings of the 'Best late-night study spot' poll onto the end, and render the whole recap as one plain-text block on screen that I can copy straight into a chat. Anything a mod has hidden stays out of the math, obviously.

The list has to react the instant the text changes — not on submit — and multiple catches show side by side, each clearing on its own as its text goes away. The moment a proposal reaches 3 endorsements it graduates on its own: it becomes a real topic in the forum, shows up among the Post Finder's topic ticks, and gets its own Campus Pulse entry right away, its tally reading ^0 rather than the quiet line — a brand-new topic should look open for business, not missing. Opening a post anywhere in the app knocks it out of the queue on the spot. Set me up already following Dorm Life and Cafeteria, with 'Quiet hours petition' and 'Meal plan swap thread' already marked as opened by me — I've read those.
