target_app_summary: What began as a bare anonymous campus forum has grown into a full community platform. Analytics arrived first: a Campus Pulse page rolls every post up by topic with whole-semester versus recent-weeks rankings, and a copyable Week in Review digest later distilled each topic's week-over-week momentum — climbing, cooling, or steady — with live poll standings appended. Community tooling grew alongside: a Poll Studio with keystroke-validated poll creation and one-decimal vote shares, a report-review-hide moderation pipeline whose hides propagate into Pulse, the digest's momentum math, and the reading queue, and a Suggest-a-Topic endorsement pipeline that graduates new topics into the forum, the Post Finder, and Pulse simultaneously. Power reading came via a multi-criteria Post Finder with saved filter combos and a Catch-up reading queue that lines up unopened posts from followed topics oldest-week-first, while a live privacy guard on the composer protects the anonymity the platform promises. A five-page visual refresh (olive pill buttons, centered underlined titles, bordered cards, tally chips, topic badges) unified it all. The feature graph is hub-heavy on the base forum and the Pulse rollups, with a three-deep chain running from forum posts through moderation hides into the momentum digest and the catch-up queue.

follow_ups.instruction: Traffic's picking up, so give me a Topics hub — a page of tag cards where each card shows how many questions the tag has and how many are still waiting on an answer, busiest tag first (alphabetical order only when two are even), and clicking a card shows just that tag's questions. follow_ups.feature_rationale: Duplicate questions are the number-one rot in a growing Q&A archive, so the ask experience needs live duplicate surfacing and posting validation.
follow_ups.instruction: People keep re-asking things we've already covered, so bolt some smarts onto the existing question form — let's call it the Ask flow from now on. As I type a title, check it live against the existing questions and show any that share a word (someone typing 'basil' should see the basil question surface before they post a duplicate), with a character count ticking along. Also gate what gets posted: nothing goes through unless the title is at least 15 characters and exactly one topic tag is chosen — call out what's missing right where I'm typing. A posted question should land in the main list and its tag's numbers on the Topics hub should follow along. And from here on, everywhere in this app now and for anything later: if something's about to be deleted or removed, ask me to confirm first.

target_app_summary: The little beige Q&A site has grown into a full community knowledge platform. Discovery grew a Topics hub of tag rollups and a validating Ask flow with live duplicate detection; recognition grew a stars-earned Contributors leaderboard that everything else plugs into — a flag-and-uphold moderation queue that claws scores back, a bounty board that pays points forward, and a digest composer that crowns a contributor of the week. Personal workflow grew a grouped watchlist with an always-consistent nav counter, and the whole thing got a consistent parchment-and-olive restyle. The feature graph funnels into the leaderboard (requests 5, 8, 9 all lean on it) and terminates in a points ledger that must reconcile every rating, bounty, and moderation event back to the leaderboard totals — a chain running four deep from the base app's ratings.

instruction: Please implement a cryptocurrency escrow system for secure cryptocurrency transactions. Buyers should be able to browse and select sellers' cryptocurrency products, conduct transactions, and deposit cryptocurrencies into an escrow account. Sellers should be able to view and manage their products and transaction records. The system should also have transaction confirmation, cryptocurrency release, and dispute resolution functionalities. Initialize the background color with light gray and component color with dark red.

ui_instruct.task: Browse the list of available cryptocurrency products.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The buyer can view a list of products with clear details like name, price, and seller information.

ui_instruct.task: Initiate a transaction by selecting a cryptocurrency product and attempting to deposit the equivalent amount into the escrow account.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The system successfully processes the deposit into the escrow account.

ui_instruct.task: Add a new cryptocurrency product.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The product is successfully added and immediately appears in the seller's product list.

ui_instruct.task: Submit a dispute for a transaction.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The dispute is lodged successfully, and the status of the transaction is updated to 'disputed'.

ui_instruct.task: Verify that the website uses 'light gray' as the background color and 'dark red' as the component color, as specified in the design requirements.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website has a background color of 'light gray' and components (such as buttons, cards, headers, etc.) are styled with the color 'dark red', accurately reflecting the design instruction.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Escrow fees are the first question every buyer and seller asks before committing funds; a live tiered quote removes the biggest pre-deal friction.
follow_ups.instruction: People always ask me upfront what the escrow cut will be, so give me a Fee Calculator page: I type a deal amount in USD and it works out our tiered fee live as I type each digit — 2.5% on the first $1,000, 1.5% on the next $4,000, and 0.75% on anything past $5,000 — with a buyer/seller split shown too, each side paying half, and when the fee lands on an odd cent the buyer eats the extra cent. So typing 1234 should read $28.51 total, $14.26 buyer and $14.25 seller, and an emptied or garbage field should just calmly show zero, not errors. Also put a small fee-preview link on each product listing that jumps into the calculator with that listing's price already filled in. One thing for everywhere in this app, now and for anything we build later: dollar amounts always show like $1,234.56 — dollar sign, thousands commas, exactly two decimals.

ui_instruct.task: Open the Fee Calculator page and type 1234 into the deal amount field.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The tiered fee shows a total of $28.51, split as $14.26 for the buyer and $14.25 for the seller — the buyer's half is exactly one cent more.

ui_instruct.task: On the Fee Calculator, type 6400 into the deal amount field.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The total fee reads $95.50 — the three tiers combined (2.5% of the first $1,000, 1.5% of the next $4,000, 0.75% of the remaining $1,400) — not a single flat-percentage figure.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The fee updates on each keystroke without any submit button, reads $12.50 once 500 is entered, and after clearing the field the calculator shows a calm zero/empty result with no NaN or error text.

ui_instruct.task: Open any cryptocurrency product listing in the marketplace and click its fee preview link.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The Fee Calculator opens with that listing's price already filled into the amount field and its tiered fee displayed, formatted like $1,234.56.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The seller's product and its information are visible, and a buyer has some visible way to select it and proceed toward a purchase/escrow transaction — however the marketplace presents that.

follow_ups.instruction: Next up: one Deal Ledger page showing every escrow deal across the whole marketplace, not buried per seller. Load it with exactly these seven to start — I'll add more later: DL-101 CryptoNova sold 0.05 BTC to aria_w for $3,200, Released, May 2026; DL-102 BlockBarn sold 10 ETH to tomcat for $18,500, Released, May 2026; DL-103 CryptoNova sold 400 SOL to nia.b for $6,400, Disputed, June 2026; DL-104 LedgerLegend sold 0.25 BTC to marko for $16,000, Released, June 2026; DL-105 BlockBarn sold 1.2 BTC to aria_w for $76,800, In Escrow, June 2026; DL-106 LedgerLegend sold 55 SOL to tomcat for $881, Refunded, June 2026; DL-107 CryptoNova sold 5 ETH to priya for $9,250, In Escrow, June 2026. Let me narrow by coin, by seller, and by ticking any mix of statuses, all of those combining together, with a totals strip that always shows the deal count and USD sum of exactly what's on screen — and when a combo matches nothing it should calmly read 0 deals and $0.00 instead of breaking. New escrow deals people start through the marketplace should land in here too. And status colors, everywhere they ever appear in this app from now on: Released green, In Escrow amber, Disputed dark red, Refunded gray.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Escrow only earns trust if contested deals get a structured, visible arbitration path instead of ad-hoc back-and-forth.
follow_ups.instruction: Buyers can already flag a deal as disputed, but then it just sits there going nowhere, so build me a proper Dispute Resolution Center. Any deal in the ledger sitting Disputed shows up there automatically as a numbered case — nobody should have to file the same complaint twice. Opening a case shows the deal's facts pulled from the ledger plus an evidence thread where the buyer and the seller each add written statements. An arbiter can't rule until both sides have at least one statement on the thread, and the ruling itself needs a written note of at least 20 characters plus a pick — refund the buyer or release to the seller. The moment a verdict lands, the deal flips to Refunded or Released over in the ledger and the case moves into a resolved archive that keeps the outcome and the ruling note. Seed CASE-1 on DL-103 with reason 'Item not delivered', already carrying one statement from buyer nia.b and one from CryptoNova, so it's ready to rule. House rule from here on, everywhere in the app: anything final or irreversible — verdicts, approvals, deletions — asks for an explicit confirmation before it actually happens.

ui_instruct.expected_result: Exactly two rows remain — DL-101 and DL-104 — and the totals strip reads 2 deals and $19,200.00; the two filters combine (not all three Released deals, and not both BTC deals plus others).

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Buyers choosing between sellers need an at-a-glance trust signal computed from real deal outcomes, not marketing copy.
follow_ups.instruction: Buyers keep asking which sellers to trust, so I want a Seller Reputation leaderboard. Score each seller by completion rate — released deals divided by all their closed deals, where closed means Released, Refunded or Disputed, and anything still In Escrow stays out of the math entirely — and show each seller's rate alongside their total released USD volume. Rank highest rate first, and when two sellers tie, the bigger released volume goes on top. With today's ledger that should come out BlockBarn at 100%, then LedgerLegend, then CryptoNova, both at 50%. target_app_summary: The base crypto escrow marketplace has grown into a full trust-and-trade platform. Tooling arrived first: a live tiered Fee Calculator wired to product listings and a Terms Configurator that saves reusable escrow term templates and shows the ledger's live In-Escrow exposure. An analytics spine grew from a pinned Deal Ledger (7 exact seeded deals with combinable coin/seller/status filters and live totals) into a Seller Reputation leaderboard with tie-broken ranking and a month-by-month seller Statement Builder that reuses the calculator's fee tiers. Workflows span surfaces: a Dispute Resolution Center that turns Disputed ledger deals into evidence-threaded arbitration cases whose gated verdicts flip ledger statuses and move reputation scores, a Seller Verification program that computes per-seller eligibility checklists live from ledger outcomes and grants (or revokes) Verified badges on the leaderboard and marketplace, and an Offers/counteroffer negotiation flow that attaches saved term templates and lands accepted offers in the ledger as new escrow deals. An Ember Vault restyle unifies five pages, and three silent conventions (USD formatting, status badge colors, confirm-before-final-actions) bind every surface. The graph's deepest chain runs base -> ledger -> disputes -> reputation -> verification.

target_app_summary: The base short-term apartment rental site (browse, search/filter, book, view booking records) grows into a full rental platform. Guest-facing, it gains a live stay cost estimator with long-stay discounting and service fees, a side-by-side compare view with per-guest value math, reviews with a tie-aware Top Rated ranking, promo codes that plug into the estimator's pricing pipeline, and a copyable trip summary composer. Operationally, bookings gain a modify/cancel workflow with a repriced review step that also seeds the booking history, an owner dashboard rolls up nights and revenue per apartment, and a guest rewards page converts that history into points, tiers, and a 100-point voucher redemption. The estimator is the pricing engine that the modification flow, dashboard, promos, and trip summaries all consume, and the booking records chain R1 -> R4 -> (R7, R9) -> R10 makes early breakage compound; a design restyle unifies the four main surfaces.

global_rules.rule: Every dollar amount anywhere in the app displays as whole dollars with a $ sign and comma thousands separators (e.g. $1,033).

follow_ups.instruction: Before anyone buys training they always ask us 'what's the return?' — so I want an ROI calculator page. Gain has to stay between 0 and 100 and team size must be a whole number of at least 1 — anything else gets a clear message, not weird math. Let me save a setup under a name and pull it back up later, and save one for me right away called Leadership Q1: 12 people, $95 an hour, $1,200 per person, 3% gain. Oh, and everywhere on this site — now and for anything we add later — dollar figures should be whole dollars with comma separators like $68,400, never cents.

follow_ups.instruction: I keep rewriting the same email for different people — build me a merge studio: I write a subject and body with placeholders like {{first_name}} and {{company}}, pick one of my contacts, and watch the merged result update live with every keystroke, plus a running count of any placeholders that didn't resolve (a typo like {{firstnme}} should stay visible as-is in the preview and get counted, not vanish). Let me pull any saved template in as a starting point, and save one for me now called Welcome Note with the subject 'Welcome to {{company}}'. Load in my actual list — exactly these six, I'll grow it later: Ana Ruiz <ana@vela.io> at Vela Systems, Customer, engagement 82; Priya Nair <priya@northbeam.dev> at Northbeam, Customer, 82; Tom Alder <tom@brightpath.org> at Brightpath, Customer, 29; Marcus Webb <marcus@treeline.co> at Treeline Co, Prospect, 41; Elif Kaya <elif@quantcove.com> at Quantcove, Prospect, 55; Jonas Silva <jonas@ferro.io> at Ferro Labs, Partner, 67. Two things I want everywhere in this app, now and for anything we add later: tag pills colored green for Customer, orange for Prospect, and blue for Partner, and any list of contacts sorted A to Z by first name unless I explicitly ask for a different order on a specific view.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: After a real campaign got spam-flagged, users need a pre-send risk meter; a rules-based live scorer catches the problem while the subject is being typed.
follow_ups.instruction: Our Partner Update got flagged as spam and I'd like to catch that before sending next time. Build me a spam-risk page with two halves. First, a risk report: every campaign I have, listed with its subject, a computed risk score, and a verdict badge right on the row. Second, a rewrite workspace: clicking a campaign in the report opens its subject there for editing (or I can start from a blank subject), and as I type, an itemized breakdown updates with every keystroke — one line per triggered rule showing the points it contributes. The rules: 2 points for each appearance of FREE, WINNER, ACT NOW, or GUARANTEED in any casing, 1 point per exclamation mark, and 3 extra points if the entire subject is in capitals. Verdicts: Low for 0-3, Medium for 4-7, High for 8 and up, everywhere a score appears.

ui_instruct.expected_result: March Promo ('Spring savings are here!') scores 1 with verdict Low, and Partner Update ('FREE partner toolkit inside!!') scores 4 — 2 for FREE plus 2 exclamation marks — with verdict Medium.

target_app_summary: The base email-sending app has grown into a full small-team outreach suite. A merge studio gives live per-keystroke personalization over a pinned six-contact book, feeding a campaign pipeline with tag-based recipient selection, merged-preview review, queue confirmation, and status tracking. Around that core grew an engagement analytics leaderboard with tag rollups, a suppression center that silently reshapes every recipient count downstream, a spam-risk page whose report scores every campaign subject and whose rewrite workspace itemizes triggered rules per keystroke, copyable on-screen campaign recaps that cross-reference current suppression, drip sequences with strict day-offset validation and suppression-aware enrollment, and per-contact profiles that aggregate campaign history, suppression status, and sequence enrollment. A late 'Harvest' restyle unifies all surfaces (forest-green primary actions, uppercase titles, white cards, pill badges) while preserving the app-wide tag-color and ordering conventions. The graph runs one deep spine — templates -> campaigns -> suppression -> sequences -> profiles — with analytics, spam checking, and recaps branching off it.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: As the registry outgrows one-by-one ID lookups, operations staff need to slice the whole product list by category, status and value in one place.
follow_ups.instruction: The registry's getting real traffic now, so I need a proper screener page where I can slice the whole product list — tick several categories at once, pick a status, and type a minimum and maximum value, all narrowing together. Start me off with exactly these six, I'll add more later: Alpine Honey HN-4102, Food from Switzerland, $1,240, 3 checkpoints, In Transit; Cedar Soap CS-2210, Cosmetics from Lebanon, $860, 5 checkpoints, Delivered; Nova Headphones NH-7731, Electronics from China, $5,400, 2 checkpoints, In Transit; Silk Scarves SS-9004, Textiles from India, $2,150, 5 checkpoints, Delivered; Oak Barrels OB-1188, Materials from France, $3,300, 4 checkpoints, Flagged; Berry Jam BJ-6520, Food from Poland, $940, 3 checkpoints, Delivered. Keep a live count that always matches the visible rows, let me save a filter combo as a named preset I can reapply in one click, and make sure the registration form captures category and declared value so anything newly registered lands straight in the screener too. Oh, and two house rules from here on out, everywhere in this app and anything we add later: dollar amounts always get a $ sign and thousands commas with whole dollars only, and statuses always appear as small colored pills — amber for In Transit, green for Delivered, red for Flagged.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: With more teams registering products, inconsistent ad-hoc IDs are breaking lookups; a live composer/checker standardizes the ID scheme before bad IDs enter the registry.
follow_ups.instruction: Our IDs need discipline, so build me an ID Workbench: I type a product name and a 4-digit sequence and it composes the ID live with every keystroke — initials of the first two words, uppercased, a dash, then the digits, so 'Berry Jam' with 6520 gives BJ-6520, and a one-word name like 'Honey' just takes its first two letters, HO. And since we keep nearly minting the same ID twice, the moment the composed ID matches one already in our registry, flag it right there as a taken ID naming which product holds it, so I never mint a collision. Give it a checker too where I paste any ID and it says on the spot whether it's well-formed — exactly two letters, a dash, exactly four digits — with a specific reason when it isn't. And a standing preference: everywhere in this app, now and in whatever we build later, IDs always display uppercase in that two-letters-dash-four-digits shape.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Quality problems currently live in email threads; filing, reviewing and resolving incidents inside the app is the natural next step and gives every product a trustworthy Flagged state.
follow_ups.instruction: Quality problems keep surfacing over email and it's a mess — I want incident management in the app. From any product's tracking page I can report an incident and see that product's existing incidents listed right there: pick a severity (Low, Medium or High), write a description of at least 15 characters — block me with a clear message if it's shorter — then show me a review screen of exactly what I'm filing before I confirm. Filed incidents collect on their own Incidents page as Open; while a product has any open incident it shows as Flagged everywhere, and resolving the last open one (with a short resolution note) flips it back to whatever it was before. Seed one that's already open: Oak Barrels, 'Cracked staves found at Lyon warehouse inspection', severity High — and when that gets resolved, Oak Barrels goes back to In Transit, which is where it was.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Handoffs between supply-chain partners are where traceability breaks; a formal transfer workflow with ID validation and incident gating keeps the circulation path authoritative.
follow_ups.instruction: Handoffs between partners are where our trail goes dark, so build a Transfers area. First, the circulation paths are patchy, so lay them down properly: each product's path gets exactly one named stop per checkpoint it has in the registry — Alpine Honey through Bern Apiary in Bern, Basel Depot in Basel and Zurich Hub in Zurich; Cedar Soap through Beirut Workshop in Beirut, Tripoli Depot in Tripoli, Piraeus Port in Piraeus, Milan Warehouse in Milan and Paris Boutique in Paris; Nova Headphones through just Shenzhen Factory in Shenzhen and Rotterdam Port in Rotterdam; Silk Scarves through Varanasi Loom in Varanasi, Mumbai Port in Mumbai, Suez Transit in Suez, Athens Depot in Athens and London Shop in London; Oak Barrels through Cognac Cooperage in Cognac, Lyon Warehouse in Lyon, Le Havre Port in Le Havre and Dublin Distillery in Dublin; Berry Jam through Lublin Orchard in Lublin, Warsaw Packhouse in Warsaw and Gdansk Port in Gdansk. Then the workflow: I start a transfer by typing the product's ID — run it through the same well-formed check our ID Workbench uses and reject it with the checker's specific reason when it fails, and if it's well-formed but not in the registry say that too — then the destination holder's name and city, then a review page, then confirm. Confirming puts the product In Transit and parks the transfer as Pending; hitting Mark received appends the destination as the newest stop on that product's circulation path and flips it to Delivered. One hard rule: a product with an open incident can't be transferred — stop me with an explanation if I try. Seed one mid-flight so the page isn't empty: Nova Headphones NH-7731 heading to Hamburg Audio in Hamburg, still Pending.

follow_ups.instruction: Insurers keep quoting us all over the map, so I want our own coverage estimator: I type a declared value and a number of transit legs and pick a category — or just pick one of our registered products to prefill its value and category — and the premium recalculates live with every keystroke: 1.5% of the value plus $12 per leg, with the percentage part doubled for Electronics, rounded to the nearest whole dollar. So $860 over 3 legs in a standard category reads $49, not $48.90. Put the math breakdown under the result, and if value or legs is empty or zero show a friendly nudge instead of a nonsense number.

target_app_summary: What began as a simple product-registration-and-lookup site has grown into a full supply-chain trust platform. Operations staff now slice the registry with a multi-criteria screener with saved presets, mint and validate product IDs in an ID Workbench, and run a custody-transfer workflow that appends verified stops to each product's circulation path. Quality teams file and resolve incidents that flip product statuses app-wide, feed an origin leaderboard's traceability scores, block transfers, and drive a Chain Integrity audit page that grades every product. A coverage estimator prices insurance from declared values, and everything culminates in a consumer-facing on-screen Product Passport that composes the path, incident history, and integrity grade. The feature graph centers on the incident module: incidents feed the leaderboard, gate transfers, drive audit grades, and surface in passports, with a 4-deep chain running base app -> incidents -> integrity audit -> passport.

instruction: Please implement an e-government system for office management, infrastructure management, procurement management, personnel management, financial management, and decision-making management. The system should have functionalities for office management, infrastructure management, procurement management, personnel management, financial management, and decision-making management. Users should be able to browse related information, submit applications, approve, query status, and perform related operations. The system should also include functions such as leave, middle-level cadres leaving Shenzhen, attendance, and "five powers" management, which can design and circulate corresponding forms and processes. Implement light pink for the page background and medium violet red for the elements.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: The base's bare submit-and-approve forms leave no trace of why anything was decided and no sense of money at stake — procurement needs a triage layer with reason-coded decisions, a per-request decision history, and live pending-money exposure.
follow_ups.instruction: The procurement section's bare submit-and-approve forms can stay as they are, but reviewing needs a real home — give me a dedicated review desk page: a triage queue of the pending requests where approving or rejecting one stamps a timestamped decision entry into that request's own decision history, and a rejection without a typed reason must not go through; every request gets a history panel I can open to read its full decision trail; and a summary strip up top shows how much money is sitting in pending requests, always matching the queue. While you're at it, tighten intake: block any request with no item or a zero/negative amount. Start the desk off with exactly these seven, I'll add more later: Fiber network upgrade (Infrastructure, ¥96,500, approved), Air conditioning overhaul (Infrastructure, ¥23,750, approved), Accounting software licenses (Finance, ¥36,900, approved), Staff laptops 12 units (Personnel, ¥54,000, pending), Archive scanning service (General Office, ¥54,000, rejected, its history already carrying the reason 'duplicate of last year's digitization contract'), Ergonomic office chairs (General Office, ¥18,400, pending), Fleet vehicle tires (Procurement, ¥8,200, pending). Two things I want app-wide from now on, everywhere and for anything we build later: money always in whole yuan with the ¥ sign and thousands separators (like ¥96,500), and statuses always color-coded — amber for pending, green for approved, red for rejected.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Procurement officers compare vendor quotes constantly; a live comparator that files the winner back into the queue closes the bidding loop.
follow_ups.instruction: For purchases that go out to bidding I need a comparator: three bid slots where I type each vendor's price, warranty in months, and delivery time in days, and it live-updates who's winning as I type. A slot missing any of its three numbers simply sits out of the comparison — never treat an empty box as a zero. Among the bids that are in, best on the most of the three categories takes it, a tied category counts for every bid tied on it, and a dead-even overall tie goes to the cheapest bid. Next to it, show the average approved purchase amount from the review desk as a sanity benchmark. Preload an example in the first slot so the page isn't empty — 'Shredder replacement' for General Office at ¥15,000, 12 months warranty, 5 days delivery — and give me a send-to-desk action that files the current winning bid straight into the review desk's queue as a pending request.

target_app_summary: A year on, the e-government office system has grown from a grab-bag of management forms into a full municipal operations suite centered on money and decisions. Procurement now runs through a seeded review desk layered over the base forms (triage queue, reason-coded decisions stamped into per-request history trails, live pending-exposure strip) that feeds nearly everything else: a live annual budget splitter that can prefill from approved spend, a leadership spending dashboard with plan-utilization, a vendor bid comparator that files winning bids back into the queue, and a payment ledger where approvals become payables with outstanding tracking. Governance grew its own leg: a decision chamber with quorum-gated committee voting whose seeded policy item scans the desk for affected requests, and a monthly executive briefing builder that composes dashboard rankings, finalized resolutions, and outstanding totals into an on-screen publishable digest. A five-page visual standard unifies the modules, and a cross-module records finder searches requests, decisions, and payables under composed filters. The graph is hub-and-spoke around the desk (R2), with a deep chain R1→R2→R4→R8→R9 and reconvergence at the briefing builder, restyle, and finder.

global_rules.rule: All money everywhere in the app is shown in whole yuan with the ¥ sign and thousands separators (e.g. ¥96,500), now and for anything added later.

Administrators should be able to view all employees' attendance records, perform statistics, and analysis. Specify papaya whip as the base color and dark orange for all components.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Admins can't manage attendance without knowing who works here — a roster with rates and week histories is the backbone every later module needs.
follow_ups.instruction: The clock in/out screens work, but I have no real picture of my staff. Add a directory page listing every employee with department and hourly rate, each name opening a profile page that shows their day-by-day hours for the week of March 2-6 plus the week total, and fold any clock in/out records from the existing system into that profile too — in fact, point the clock in/out screen at this same roster, so I pick which of these people is punching and the punch lands straight on their profile. Start me with exactly these six, I'll grow it later: Ana Torres (Operations, $22/hr, Mon-Fri 8/8/8/8/10), Ben Cho (Operations, $20/hr, 8/0/8/8/8), Carla Mendes (Support, $18/hr, 8/8/8/8/8), Dev Patel (Support, $18/hr, 8/8/0/0/8), Elif Kaya (Engineering, $30/hr, 9/9/9/9/9), Frank Osei (Engineering, $30/hr, 8/8/8/8/0) — a 0 means they were out that day. There should be a form to add someone new, and it shouldn't let me save without a name, a department, and a rate that's a positive number — and when something's off, tell me what's wrong right there on the form instead of quietly refusing. One preference for everywhere in this app, now and for anything we add later: any time employees get listed, keep them alphabetical by first name unless something explicitly ranks them.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Rates say what a week costs, but thin days are what blindside managers — a per-day presence board turns the raw week histories into an at-a-glance short-staffing signal.
follow_ups.instruction: Something else those week histories should tell me: which days ran thin. Build a staffing board for the March 2-6 week — a grid with a row per department and a column for each weekday, every cell counting how many people in that department actually worked that day. Someone counts as present only if they logged more than zero hours that day; merely being on the roster isn't enough. Give each department a minimum-staffing number I can edit right on the board — start all three at 2 — and mark each cell at or above its department's minimum as covered and each cell below it as short-staffed, re-marking that row the moment I change the number. And anybody added to the directory later with no hours logged that week must leave every cell's count exactly where it was.

target_app_summary: The little clock-in/out tracker has grown into a full workforce-management suite for small teams. A staff directory with per-employee profiles and a pinned week of logged hours became the backbone: a live pay estimator, a daily staffing board that counts who actually worked each day and flags short-staffed cells, a leave request-and-approval center, an absence audit that reconciles zero-hour days against approved leave, a shift coverage planner with live headcount and labor-cost meters, and a payroll preview that rolls hours, overtime, and approved paid leave into exact dollar rows. A design refresh unifies the now five-plus pages, and a records explorer lets admins slice every day-entry by department, excused/unexcused verdict, and minimum hours. The graph is hub-and-spoke around the directory seed, with one deep chain: directory records feed the leave center, whose decisions drive the absence audit, whose verdicts power the records explorer's status filter and the payroll's paid-leave credits.

instruction: Please implement a health survey website for women to fill out and submit health information. The website should have functionalities for filling out the survey, and submitting information. Users can fill out the relevant survey, and submit their information. The system will automatically collect the information and provide data management, permission management, data review, and reporting functions. Use whitesmoke as the default background and dark cyan for component styling.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Survey takers want instant meaning from their answers; a live score panel rewards completion and is the first thing respondents would ask this tool for.
follow_ups.instruction: People filling out the survey keep asking what their numbers actually mean, so add a live wellness panel right on the form. As a woman types her height in cm, weight in kg, average nightly sleep hours, and exercise days per week, show her BMI rounded to one decimal and a wellness score out of 100 that updates with every keystroke: 40 points if BMI lands from 18.5 up to but not including 25, 20 points from 25 up to 30, 10 otherwise; 30 points for 7 or more hours of sleep, 15 for 5 to under 7, 5 below that; and 30 points for 4 or more exercise days, 15 for 2 or 3, 5 for 0 or 1. Label the score with a band — 75 and up is Good, 50 to 74 is Watch, under 50 is Needs attention — and everywhere in this app, now and for anything we build later, show those bands as small colored pills: green for Good, amber for Watch, red for Needs attention. Before anything's typed the panel should sit quietly with placeholders, never NaN or an error, and when she submits, her score and band go along with her submission.

ui_instruct.expected_result: Before any input the panel shows a neutral placeholder state (no NaN, no error), and with only sleep filled it still shows no NaN — BMI stays a placeholder until both height and weight are present.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The submission completes with visible confirmation, and the wellness panel showing 80 with a Good pill does not block or break the survey's submit flow.

Across the survey page, the triage queue, the clinic comparison, the screener, and the follow-ups page: give every page a dark cyan header band with the page title in white sitting on the left; make every primary action button pill-shaped; put cards and tiles on 12px rounded corners with a soft shadow; set section headings in uppercase with a little letter spacing; and stripe list and table rows in alternating whitesmoke and white. All five pages get the same treatment — none left on the old look — and leave our green, amber and red band pills exactly as they are.

ui_instruct.expected_result: It has a dark cyan header band with the page title in white on the left, and its three rows — Eastview Health, then Northside Clinic, then Riverbend Center — are striped in alternating whitesmoke and white.

ui_instruct.task: Look at the survey page's submit control and then at the action buttons on the follow-ups page.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Staff currently hop across three pages to understand one woman's situation; a joined profile view is the natural capstone over submissions, reviews and cases.
follow_ups.instruction: Last big one — tie each woman's whole story together. Wherever her name appears, on triage queue rows or on follow-up cases, let me click it to open her profile: one page with her survey details and wellness score with its band pill, her review status (including the return reason if she was returned), and her follow-up case history with statuses and outcome notes, oldest first. And when a section has nothing to show — say she's never had a follow-up case — give me a friendly nothing-here-yet note for that section, never a blank hole or an error.

ui_instruct.task: From the triage queue, click Amara Diallo's name to open her profile.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Her profile shows score 58 with an amber Watch pill, a returned review status with the reason 'missing blood pressure reading', and one Contacted follow-up case in her history.

ui_instruct.task: From the triage queue, open Maya Okafor's profile.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Her score 82 with a green Good pill and her approved status render fine, and the follow-up section shows an explicit nothing-here-yet style note — the page neither errors nor leaves that section blank.

ui_instruct.task: From the triage queue, open Priya Shah's profile.
ui_instruct.expected_result: It shows her pending review status, score 64 with an amber Watch pill, and her Closed follow-up case with the outcome 'scheduled clinic visit'.

ui_instruct.task: On the follow-ups page, click Lena Vogel's name on her case to open her profile.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The same profile page opens showing her Open case, score 47 with a red Needs attention pill, and her approved review status — the case list and the triage queue lead to one consistent profile.

ui_instruct.task: Open the program reconciliation page on a fresh load and read the review completion and follow-up resolution rates.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Review completion reads 71.4% (5 of 7 — the 4 approved plus Amara Diallo's returned one, since a return still counts as reviewed) and follow-up resolution reads 33.3% (1 of 3 cases closed) — each with one decimal place, and completion is not 57.1%, which would mean returned submissions were wrongly left out.

target_app_summary: A simple women's health survey form has grown into a full community-health program platform. The survey itself gained a keystroke-live wellness score with BMI and band pills, and everything submitted now lands in a risk triage queue ranked most-at-risk first and seeded with seven exact records — the app's data spine. On top of that spine sit an approve-or-return vetting gate with required reasons and confirmations, a clinic comparison that ranks only review-approved data, a multi-criteria outreach screener with a copyable call list, and follow-up cases that carry screened women from Open to a noted Closed while joining each woman's score, clinic and band from her submission. A reconciliation page cross-checks review completion, case resolution and outreach coverage as live rates, a dark-cyan visual system unifies all five surfaces, and a respondent profile joins each woman's submission, review outcome and case history onto one page. The graph is hub-and-spoke around the triage queue with two deep chains — base app -> queue -> vetting gate -> clinic comparison, and queue -> screener -> cases -> reconciliation — so early breakage compounds.

instruction: Please implement a recruitment website for hiring drivers and posting job listings. The website should have functionalities for user registration, job posting, job application, and contact form. Users should be able to register and create profiles, apply for jobs, and manage their contact information. Clients should be able to view their active job postings. The website should include pages such as home, about us, clients, drivers, jobs, and contact. Design the site using white as the background and navy for content blocks.

ui_instruct.task: Test user registration form submission.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A new user profile is created successfully, and a confirmation message is displayed indicating registration completion.

ui_instruct.task: Test job posting functionality for clients.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A new job listing is created and appears in the list of active job postings with correct details.

ui_instruct.task: Verify that users can apply for a job listing.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The user's application is submitted successfully, and confirmation is displayed to the user.

ui_instruct.task: Check that users can update their contact information.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Changes to the contact information are saved, and a confirmation message is displayed to the user.

ui_instruct.task: Validate that the contact form can be submitted.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The contact form submission succeeds, and a thank you message is displayed to the user.

ui_instruct.task: Confirm navigation from the home page to the 'About Us' page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Clicking the 'About Us' link takes the user to the 'About Us' page without any errors.

ui_instruct.task: Verify accessibility of the home page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The home page is accessible.

ui_instruct.task: Check the ability for clients to view all their active job postings.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The client can see a list of all active job postings with correct and up-to-date information.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The website has a background color of 'white' and components (such as buttons, cards, headers, etc.) are styled with the color 'navy', accurately reflecting the design instruction.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Drivers evaluating postings priced in cents-per-mile need to see what a week actually pays before they bother applying.
follow_ups.instruction: Drivers keep asking what these postings actually mean for a paycheck, so give them a take-home estimator on its own page: they type a rate in cents per mile, miles per week, an optional weekly bonus in dollars, and an estimated expenses percentage, and it shows weekly take-home — miles times the rate, plus the bonus, then minus the expenses cut — plus a yearly figure at 52 weeks, all updating as they type with no submit button. If a field is empty just treat it as zero; never show NaN or a blank number. And one thing for everywhere in this app, now and for anything we add later: dollar amounts get a $ sign and commas and are rounded to whole dollars — per-mile rates stay in cents, written like 62¢/mi.

ui_instruct.task: Open the take-home estimator page and type 62 into the rate field, 2000 into the miles per week field, 150 into the weekly bonus field, and 10 into the expenses percentage field.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Weekly take-home shows $1,251 and the yearly figure shows $65,052 — the expenses cut is applied after the bonus is added, not before.

ui_instruct.task: With 62, 2000, 150, and 10 entered in the estimator, clear the miles per week field completely.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Weekly take-home updates to $135 (just the bonus minus the 10% cut) with no NaN, blank, or error shown.

ui_instruct.expected_result: Weekly take-home reads $500 and updates while the values are typed, without pressing any submit or calculate button.

ui_instruct.expected_result: Weekly shows $1,240 and yearly shows $64,480 — both with a $ sign and comma-separated thousands, rounded to whole dollars with no decimals.

follow_ups.instruction: The jobs page needs to grow into a proper job board. Load it with exactly these seven openings and no others for now — I'll add more later: Redline Freight (OTR, CDL-A, 68¢/mi, 2,600 mi/wk, Hazmat required); Bluegrass Haulers (Regional, CDL-A, 62¢/mi, 2,200 mi/wk); Metro Parcel (Local, CDL-B, 54¢/mi, 1,400 mi/wk); Cascade Logistics (OTR, CDL-A, 62¢/mi, 2,500 mi/wk); Harbor Line Transport (Regional, CDL-B, 54¢/mi, 1,800 mi/wk); Prairie Express (Regional, CDL-A, 59¢/mi, 2,000 mi/wk, Hazmat required); Summit Carriers (OTR, CDL-A, 71¢/mi, 2,400 mi/wk, Tanker required). Drivers filter by route type (checking several means any of those), by required license class, and by a minimum rate typed in cents — the filters stack together, with a little 'Showing X of 7' line that stays honest as they change. Default order is highest rate first, and when two jobs pay the same, alphabetical by company. Also a look thing that should hold everywhere in the app from now on: wherever a route type shows up, badge it — Local in green, Regional in orange, OTR in navy.

Highest rate isn't always the best week, so this matters. target_app_summary: A year on, the driver-recruitment site has grown from a brochure-with-forms into a full hiring marketplace for trucking. Drivers get a take-home pay estimator, a seeded seven-listing job board with stacking route/license/rate filters and tie-aware pay sorting, a three-job compare workspace wired into the estimator, a qualification profile that live-computes eligibility (CDL-A covering CDL-B, endorsement gating), and a copyable pay report — top rate, best weekly money, and pay spread — generated from whatever the board's filters currently show. Clients get a validated application pipeline (Submitted through Offer) with a review queue, a hiring dashboard whose stage totals and most-applied rankings stay in lockstep with that queue, and an offer flow whose acceptance flips jobs to Filled back on the board. A late restyle rolls a safety-orange/navy visual language consistently across all six major surfaces. The feature graph is hub-shaped around the job board (R3), which feeds the pipeline, compare, eligibility, offers, the dashboard's rate aggregates, and the report, with a four-deep chain running base app -> job board -> pipeline -> dashboard.

instruction: Please implement a web application for one-to-one coaching sessions to match coaches and users. The application should have functionalities such as personality assessment, user profiles, coaching and mentorship matching, scheduling and session management, and goal setting and progress tracking. Users should be able to complete a personality assessment, create and manage their profiles, search for and select suitable coaches, schedule coaching sessions, and set and track goals. Set the background to beige, and apply saddle brown to components.

ui_instruct.task: Assess the personality assessment functionality by completing the full assessment.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The system should display an assessment summary or results, and these results should be saved to the user’s profile.

ui_instruct.task: Examine the profile creation feature by updating the user profile information.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Updated profile details should be saved correctly and displayed on the user profile page.

ui_instruct.task: Check the coaching and mentorship matching feature by searching for available coaches.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The system should list suitable coaches based on user preferences and assessment results.

ui_instruct.task: Test scheduling a new coaching session with a selected coach.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The session should be added to the user’s and coach’s calendars, and both parties should receive a confirmation notification.

ui_instruct.task: Evaluate goal-setting and progress tracking by creating and updating a personal goal.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The goal should be saved successfully, and progress updates should reflect accurately in the system.

ui_instruct.task: Verify that the website uses 'beige' as the background color and 'saddle brown' as the component color, as specified in the design requirements.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website has a background color of 'beige' and components (such as buttons, cards, headers, etc.) are styled with the color 'saddle brown', accurately reflecting the design instruction.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Coachees accumulate sessions across several coaches and need one auditable record of time, money and value to judge whether coaching is paying off.
follow_ups.instruction: Now that I've had a bunch of sessions, I want a Session Journal page where every completed session lives — coach, date, focus area, how long it ran, what I paid, and my 1-5 rating — with a summary up top showing total time, total spent, and my average rating to one decimal like 4.2/5, plus a focus-area filter that keeps the summary matching whatever's actually shown. Start me off with exactly these six, I'll add more later: Career Clarity with Dana Reyes, Mar 3 2025, Career, 60 min, $90, rated 5; Confidence Kickoff with Marcus Bell, Mar 18, Confidence, 45 min, $60, rated 4; Career Deep Dive with Dana Reyes, Apr 2, Career, 60 min, $90, rated 4; Stress Reset with Priya Nair, Apr 20, Wellness, 90 min, $105, rated 4; Leadership Lab with Marcus Bell, May 6, Leadership, 60 min, $80, rated 3; Wellness Check with Priya Nair, May 21, Wellness, 60 min, $70, rated 5. Two things to bake in everywhere in this app, now and for anything we add later: durations always read as hours and minutes like 1h 30m (just 45m when it's under an hour, and a whole hour keeps its zero minutes — 3h 0m, never just 3h), never raw minutes, and any list with dates goes newest first.

ui_instruct.task: Open the Session Journal page and read the summary at the top.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The summary shows total time 6h 15m, total spent $495, and an average rating of 4.2/5 (not 4.1 or 4.17).

ui_instruct.task: Open the Session Journal and look at the order of the entries.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Entries are listed newest first: Wellness Check (May 21) at the top and Career Clarity (Mar 3) at the bottom.

ui_instruct.task: In the Session Journal, use the focus-area filter to show only Wellness.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Exactly two entries remain (Stress Reset and Wellness Check) and the summary updates to 2h 30m, $175, and 4.5/5.

ui_instruct.task: In the Session Journal, look at the duration shown on the Stress Reset entry.
ui_instruct.expected_result: It reads 1h 30m (hours-and-minutes style), not 90 minutes.

ui_instruct.task: Go to the goals area, create a new goal named 'Speak up more in meetings', and save it.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The new goal appears in the goals list.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Coaching is a recurring spend; users planning next month need to convert a budget and a coach's rate into an exact number of affordable sessions before committing.
follow_ups.instruction: I keep doing coaching math on napkins — build me a Budget Planner page where I type a monthly budget, a coach's hourly rate, and a session length in minutes, and it works everything out live as I type: what one session costs, how many full sessions I can afford that month, what's left over, and how much total coaching time that buys. So $300 with a $90-an-hour coach at 60 minutes should come out to 3 sessions with $30 left over. And don't let it show NaN weirdness while a box is still empty — just prompt me nicely until all three are filled in.

ui_instruct.expected_result: It shows $90 per session, 3 sessions affordable, $30 left over, and 3h 0m of total coaching time.

ui_instruct.task: With 300, 90 and 60 entered on the Budget Planner, change the hourly rate to 75.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The results update immediately with no submit step: 4 sessions, $0 left over, and 4h 0m of coaching time (exact division handled correctly).

ui_instruct.task: On the Budget Planner, fill in 300, 90 and 60, then clear the budget field.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The results area returns to a friendly prompt state — no NaN, Infinity, or crash.

ui_instruct.expected_result: It reads 3h 0m (2 sessions of 90 minutes), shown in hours-and-minutes style, never as 180 minutes.

ui_instruct.task: Open the Session Journal page and read the summary at the top.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The summary shows total time 6h 15m, total spent $495, and an average rating of 4.2/5 (not 4.1 or 4.17).

follow_ups.feature_rationale: A bare goal percent is meaningless; serious users plan weighted milestones so a goal's progress reflects the real work completed.
follow_ups.instruction: Goals are too vague on their own — let me break any of the goals I've set into weighted milestones. The flow: pick one of my goals, add milestones each with a percent weight, see a running total as I go, and get a review of the whole plan before I confirm — but don't let a plan save unless the weights add up to exactly 100, and let me come back into a plan later to add or tweak milestones under the same rule. On the goal itself, progress is simply the summed weights of milestones I've ticked done, and when I tick one, ask me the date I finished it. Set up my goal 'Land a team lead role' with Update resume at 20% (finished that one Apr 10, 2025), Complete leadership course at 40%, Lead two projects at 30%, and Ask for growth review at 10% — so it sits at 20% right now. Also, from here on, everywhere in this app, if I delete anything — a milestone, a journal entry, whatever we add later — ask me to confirm before it actually goes.

ui_instruct.task: Open the milestone planner and look at the goal 'Land a team lead role'.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Its progress reads 20% complete — the weight of the one finished milestone, not 25% for 1-of-4 done.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The plan cannot be saved — saving is blocked or a message says the weights must total exactly 100 — and the running total reads 115.

ui_instruct.task: In the plan for 'Land a team lead role', tick the milestone 'Complete leadership course' as done and enter May 30, 2025 as the finish date.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The goal's progress updates to 60% (20 + 40), not 50%.

ui_instruct.task: In the goals area, create a goal named 'Run a 10K', save it, then open the milestone planner.
ui_instruct.expected_result: 'Run a 10K' is available to plan milestones for, showing 0% progress.

ui_instruct.task: Open the Session Journal and look at the order of the entries.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Entries are listed newest first: Wellness Check (May 21) at the top and Career Clarity (Mar 3) at the bottom.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: With sessions spread across several coaches, users need to see which coach actually delivers value before deciding who to rebook.

Rank the cards best average first, and when two coaches tie on average, whoever has more time with me goes on top. Also give me a way to delete an entry right from the Session Journal — sometimes I log one by mistake — and if I ever delete or add a journal entry, the cards should just follow.

ui_instruct.task: Open the Coach Scorecards page and read the order of the cards from top to bottom.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Priya Nair first, then Dana Reyes, then Marcus Bell — Priya and Dana both average 4.5/5, and Priya's greater total time (2h 30m vs 2h 0m) puts her on top.

ui_instruct.task: On Coach Scorecards, read Dana Reyes's card.
ui_instruct.expected_result: It shows 2 sessions, 2h 0m total time, $180 paid, and a 4.5/5 average.

ui_instruct.task: On Coach Scorecards, read Marcus Bell's card.
ui_instruct.expected_result: It shows 2 sessions, 1h 45m total time, and a 3.5/5 average.

ui_instruct.task: In the Session Journal, delete the Wellness Check entry (confirm when asked), then open Coach Scorecards.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A confirmation was required before the delete, and Priya's card now reads 1 session, 1h 30m, 4.0/5, so the order becomes Dana Reyes, Priya Nair, Marcus Bell.

ui_instruct.task: On the Budget Planner, type 300 into the monthly budget, 90 into the hourly rate, and 60 into the session length.
ui_instruct.expected_result: It shows $90 per session, 3 sessions affordable, $30 left over, and 3h 0m of total coaching time.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Coaching time drifts toward whatever felt urgent that week; comparing logged hours against quarterly targets per focus area shows where the mix is off while there's still time to fix it.
follow_ups.instruction: I suspect my coaching hours are lopsided across focus areas. Give me a Focus Balance page: every focus area from my journal shows up as a clickable chip — Career, Confidence, Wellness, Leadership — and I toggle on the ones I want to plan around. A toggled-on area shows the actual time I've logged with that focus, pulled straight from my Session Journal so it always agrees with it, next to a box where I type my target for the quarter in hours. Everything recalculates as I type, no submit button: what percent of the target I've hit as a whole number, and whether I'm ahead of or behind the target and by how much. If I've hit a target exactly, just say I'm on target — no zero-gap weirdness — and an area I've toggled on but haven't given a target yet should just show its actual time and nudge me to set one.

ui_instruct.task: On the Focus Balance page, toggle on the Career chip and type 3 into its quarterly target.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Career shows 2h 0m of actual logged time against the 3-hour target, 67% of target (not 66%), and reads as behind by 1h 0m.

ui_instruct.task: With Career toggled on and 3 typed as its target, change the target to 2.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The results update immediately with no submit step: Career reads 100% of target and is reported as on target — not 'behind by 0m' or any negative-zero oddity.

ui_instruct.task: On the Focus Balance page, toggle on Wellness and Confidence, type 2 as Wellness's target and 1 as Confidence's target.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Wellness shows 2h 30m actual, 125% of target, ahead by 30m; Confidence shows 45m actual, 75% of target, behind by 15m — both updating live as the targets are typed.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Session insights evaporate by dinner; a guided debrief turns each scheduled session into a validated journal record while it's still fresh.
follow_ups.instruction: I keep forgetting how sessions went — give me a debrief flow. I've got two coming up: Career Clarity follow-up with Dana Reyes on Jun 2, 2025 (Career, 60 minutes, $90) and Leadership Lab II with Marcus Bell on Jun 9 (Leadership, 60 minutes, $80) — list those somewhere as upcoming, each with a debrief button. Debriefing pre-fills the coach, date, focus, length and price from the session; I add a 1-5 rating (nothing outside 1 to 5, and don't let me move on without one) plus an optional takeaway note, then a review screen shows the whole entry so I can go back or confirm. Only on confirm does it land in my Session Journal in its proper date spot, with all the journal numbers updating.

ui_instruct.task: Complete a debrief for the Jun 9 session with Marcus Bell (rate it 4, continue, confirm), then look at the top of the Session Journal.

Keep the beige background, but across the Session Journal, Coach Scorecards, Budget Planner, Milestone Planner, and Focus Balance page — every one of them, no half-done pages — make it consistent: buttons and clickable option controls go deep olive green with white text instead of saddle brown, every page heading sits left-aligned with a short saddle brown accent bar underneath it, content moves onto white cards with rounded corners and a soft shadow, focus-area and status badges become pills with white text, and the big stat numbers (totals, averages, percentages) go bold dark brown.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The goal's progress updates to 60% (20 + 40), not 50%.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Sessions and milestone wins live on separate pages; users want one chronological story of their progress, month by month.
follow_ups.instruction: I want one place that tells the whole story — a Progress Timeline that merges my completed journal sessions and my finished milestones into a single stream, grouped by month like 'May 2025'. Every month header should total up the coaching time I logged that month and how many milestones I finished. Only things that actually happened belong there — upcoming sessions stay out — and a month with sessions but no milestones should still look clean, not broken.

ui_instruct.task: On the Progress Timeline, check for a June 2025 group and read the March 2025 header.
ui_instruct.expected_result: No June 2025 group appears (the upcoming Jun 2 and Jun 9 sessions are not completed), and March's header shows 1h 45m of coaching with zero milestones, rendered cleanly.

ui_instruct.task: In the milestone planner, tick 'Lead two projects' as done and enter Jun 14, 2025 as the finish date, then open the Progress Timeline.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A June 2025 group now appears at the top of the timeline containing the 'Lead two projects' completion, counted as 1 milestone finished in its header.

ui_instruct.expected_result: Priya Nair first, then Dana Reyes, then Marcus Bell — Priya and Dana both average 4.5/5, and Priya's greater total time (2h 30m vs 2h 0m) puts her on top.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Users report progress to mentors and managers quarterly and need a copyable report that mirrors the app's live numbers exactly.
follow_ups.instruction: Quarterly check-in with my mentor is coming up — build me a Progress Report composer. Let me tick which sections to include, with all four on by default: Session Stats (session count, total time, average rating, total spent), Top Coach (whoever sits on top of the scorecards, with their average and time together), Goal Progress (each goal with its milestone-driven percent), and Latest Month (the most recent month on my Progress Timeline, restating that month's coaching-time and milestones-finished rollup exactly as the timeline's header has it — so upcoming sessions can't sneak a month in). Then it generates the report right on screen as a text block I can copy, pulling live numbers so it always matches whatever the journal, scorecards, milestone planner and timeline say at that moment. And if I untick everything, don't hand me a blank mess — just nudge me to pick at least one section.

ui_instruct.task: On the Progress Report composer, with all four sections ticked (the default), generate the report and read it.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The on-screen report shows Session Stats of 6 sessions, 6h 15m, 4.2/5 average, $495 spent; Top Coach Priya Nair at 4.5/5 over 2h 30m; 'Land a team lead role' at 20% complete; and a Latest Month section for May 2025 with 2h 0m of coaching and 0 milestones finished — May, not June, since the Jun 2 and Jun 9 sessions haven't happened yet.

ui_instruct.task: On the composer, untick the Top Coach section and generate the report.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The report contains the Session Stats, Goal Progress, and Latest Month sections but no coach section.

ui_instruct.task: On the composer, untick all four sections and try to generate.
ui_instruct.expected_result: No blank or broken report appears — generation is blocked or a message asks to pick at least one section.

ui_instruct.task: In the Session Journal, delete the Wellness Check entry (confirm when asked), then generate a full report with all four sections.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Session Stats now read 5 sessions, 5h 15m, 4.0/5, $425, the Top Coach flips to Dana Reyes at 4.5/5 (Priya drops to 4.0/5), and the Latest Month section still says May 2025 but its coaching time drops to 1h 0m.

ui_instruct.task: In the upcoming sessions list, start a debrief for the Jun 2 session with Dana Reyes, leave the rating unset, and try to continue.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The flow does not advance to the review screen — continuing is blocked or a message asks for a rating — until a 1-5 rating is given.

target_app_summary: A one-to-one coaching platform that has grown from basic matching/scheduling/goals into a full coaching-life companion. It gained an analytics spine (a seeded Session Journal with live totals, per-coach Scorecards ranked with a time-on-tie rule, and a month-grouped Progress Timeline merging sessions with milestone completions), planning tools (a live Budget Planner and a weighted Milestone Planner with 100%-validation and dated completions), a Focus Balance planner that compares typed quarterly targets against per-focus time pulled live from the journal, a workflow that closes the loop (a Debrief flow that turns scheduled sessions into validated journal entries), a copyable Progress Report composer that must mirror the live journal/scorecard/milestone numbers, and a five-page olive-and-beige visual refresh. The graph centers on the journal: debriefs write into it, scorecards aggregate it, the timeline, balance planner and report read from it, and the report also consumes the scorecard ranking, the milestone percents, and the timeline's latest-month rollup, so the graph runs three edges deep along R2-R7-R9-R10 (and R1-R4-R9-R10).

instruction: Please develop a children's recycling game website to educate kids on proper waste recycling. The game should include competitive elements such as a leaderboard to keep kids engaged and motivated. The game should use a cartoon-style visual design to make it visually appealing to children. Kids should be able to play the game, receive feedback, learn how to correctly sort waste into the corresponding containers, and receive rewards and recognition through the game. Use seashell for container backgrounds and crimson for component visuals.

ui_instruct.task: Test the functionality of starting a new game.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The game should initialize with an introductory screen displaying instructions on how to play, including sorting waste into correct containers.

ui_instruct.task: Check the leaderboard feature to ensure it displays scores correctly.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The leaderboard should show a list of players with their respective scores in descending order without any visual errors.

ui_instruct.task: Assess the cartoon-style visual design for appropriateness.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The visuals should be colorful, child-friendly, and consistent throughout the website, with no inappropriate or non-cartoonish elements present.

ui_instruct.task: Test the feedback system for incorrect sorting.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Placing a waste item in the wrong container should trigger a gentle correction prompt explaining the correct choice without being discouraging.

ui_instruct.task: Verify the awarding of rewards and recognition within the game.
ui_instruct.expected_result: After correctly sorting a designated number of items or reaching a specific score, the game should display a reward screen or badge to acknowledge the player’s achievement.

ui_instruct.task: Verify that the website uses 'seashell' as the background color and 'crimson' as the component color, as specified in the design requirements.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website has a background color of 'seashell' and components (such as buttons, cards, headers, etc.) are styled with the color 'crimson', accurately reflecting the design instruction.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: The game already ranks kids, so a teacher's very next need is a real roster with per-kid profiles that the leaderboard and every future feature can hang off.
follow_ups.instruction: The game's a hit with my class, so I need a proper roster now. Give me a roster page where each kid clicks through to their own profile showing games played, total points, and average points per game to one decimal — and start me off with exactly these six (they should feed the leaderboard too): Ben 210 pts over 4 games with his last three games scoring 30, 30, 30; Lily 520 pts over 15 games (last three: 10, 15, 20); Max 450 pts over 9 games (50, 40, 45); Mia 300 pts over 6 games (5, 10, 15); Omar 450 pts over 10 games (45, 45, 45); and Zoe 480 pts over 12 games (20, 35, 25) — I'll add more kids later. There's an add-kid form too: no blank names, no duplicates even if the capitals differ, and newcomers start at zero without their profile showing some broken average. Two things I want everywhere in this app from here on out, including anything we build later: point values always written with a pts suffix like 480 pts, and whenever kids tie on any ranking, list the tied ones alphabetically.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The game responds with visible feedback indicating whether the sort was right or wrong.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Kids ask what their points mean for the planet, so a live impact calculator turns abstract scores into CO2 and trees and makes home recycling count.
follow_ups.instruction: Kids keep asking what their points actually do for the planet, so let's show them. Build an Eco-Impact page with boxes to type how many cans, plastic bottles, and paper sheets they recycled at home — it recalculates the moment they type, no button: cans save 0.2 kg of CO2 each, bottles 0.1 kg, paper 0.05 kg, total shown to one decimal, plus how many trees' worth that equals at 1.5 kg per tree (whole trees only, always round down). Also put a picker to choose any kid from the roster and translate their points: every 10 pts earned counts as one item kept out of the trash, each item worth 0.2 kg of CO2. Empty boxes just mean zero — it shouldn't show weird numbers or fall over on a blank start, and letters or negatives shouldn't sneak in.

target_app_summary: What began as a single cartoon waste-sorting game with a leaderboard has grown into a full classroom recycling platform. A seeded six-kid roster with clickable profile pages anchors everything: an eco-impact calculator translates points into CO2 and trees, a sticker shop lets kids spend points (with an app-wide confirmation convention), and a weekly round-up digest surfaces recent three-game form instead of all-time totals. On top of these sit a head-to-head face-off comparator, a class-wide mission tracker that counts earned rather than remaining points, a live certificate maker with star ratings, and a gated eco-diploma graduation flow requiring points, games played, and a shop sticker. A deep-sea design makeover unifies every surface. The feature graph fans out from the roster (R2) and shop (R4), with chains like roster->shop->graduation and roster->round-up->face-off running three-plus deep, so early breakage compounds.

instruction: Please implement a family event portal website for publishing and storing obituaries, funeral arrangements, and multimedia memories. The website should have functionalities for obituary publishing, mortuary list, condolences, and statistics. Users should be able to publish and manage their own obituaries and funeral arrangements, view and leave messages on others' obituaries, and view statistical analysis. Use cornsilk for the outer layout and peru for UI blocks.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The obituary should be successfully published, appear on the user's dashboard, and be accessible to other users from the main obituaries page.

ui_instruct.expected_result: The list should display comprehensive details about each mortuary, including name, location, and contact information.

follow_ups.instruction: People want to do more than read - let visitors light a tribute candle right on each obituary page, and give the portal an Honor Roll page that ranks every memorial by candles lit, most first, with ties falling back to alphabetical order. Start me off with exactly these six (I'll add more later): Eleanor Vance 1938-2024 with 14 candles, Marcus Webb 1951-2024 with 9, Rosa Delgado 1946-2025 with 21, Harold Finch 1929-2025 with 9, Priya Nair 1963-2024 with 17, and Thomas Okafor 1940-2025 with 5. Lighting a candle should bump the count and re-rank the Honor Roll right away, no reload. And a habit for everywhere in this app, now and for anything we add later: whenever a person's name shows up, put their years with it, like Eleanor Vance (1938-2024).

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Grieving families' first practical question is what a service will cost - a live estimator turns the portal from a publishing site into a planning companion.
follow_ups.instruction: Families always ask what a service runs, so build a cost estimator page: choose a package - Graveside $2,200, Chapel $3,800, or Full Traditional $5,600 - type the guest count (whole numbers 1 to 500, complain about anything else), reception adds $18 a head, plus two tick-box extras: memorial flowers $250 and printed programs at $3 per guest. Then an 8% coordination fee goes on top of everything, and the final total rounds to the nearest dollar. I want the itemized breakdown recalculating as I type, not after some submit click, and let me pick which memorial the estimate is for so it's titled for them. From here on, every dollar figure anywhere in the portal is whole dollars with commas - $5,735, never cents.

follow_ups.instruction: For the service itself we hand out printed programs, so give me a program composer: I pick the memorial, type free-text lines for the order of service - opening hymn, reading, eulogy speaker - plus a dedication line capped at 120 characters with a live counter, and a preview panel beside the form re-renders with every letter I type, headed with the name of whoever the program is for, the finished program shown as copyable text right on screen. Add a toggle to pull in their published life story: flip it and the milestones drop into the program oldest first, and if someone has no published story the composer should say so instead of showing an empty block.

ui_instruct.task: In the program composer, pick Eleanor Vance and type 'Amazing Grace' into the opening hymn field.

ui_instruct.expected_result: Instead of an empty milestones block, the composer clearly indicates Thomas has no published life story, and the preview stays intact - no crash or blank panel.

ui_instruct.task: In the program composer, pick Eleanor Vance and switch on the include-life-story toggle.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The preview, headed Eleanor Vance (1938-2024), now lists her three milestones oldest first - 1956 Graduated Whitfield High, 1962 Married Arthur, 1990 Opened the bakery.

ui_instruct.task: Pick Marcus Webb in the program composer and look at the program preview's header.
