follow_ups.feature_rationale: As condolences pile up, families need to curate their guestbook - surfacing the messages that matter most and quietly removing the rest is a duty of care the portal owes them.
follow_ups.instruction: Families should curate their guestbook. Give every memorial a condolence review desk: new condolences still appear on the obituary immediately, but they land in the desk marked unreviewed until the family deals with them, and the desk shows how many are still unreviewed. From the desk they can pin one as Featured - it jumps to the top of the obituary's condolence list with a gold Featured tag, everything else ordered newest first below - or remove one, always with an are-you-sure check before anything is deleted. Seed Eleanor's with three: Ruth M. saying 'She taught me to bake', the Henderson family with 'Our street won't be the same', and Sam O. with 'A true friend'.

ui_instruct.task: Open Eleanor Vance's condolence review desk.
ui_instruct.expected_result: All three seeded condolences (Ruth M., the Henderson family, Sam O.) are listed on the desk, each wearing an amber unreviewed pill - none of them presented as reviewed or featured yet, and none of them missing.

ui_instruct.task: On Eleanor Vance's condolence review desk, mark Ruth M.'s condolence as Featured, then open Eleanor's obituary page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Ruth M.'s message 'She taught me to bake' now sits at the very top of the condolence list on the page identifying her as Eleanor Vance (1938-2024), wearing a gold Featured tag, above the Henderson family's and Sam O.'s messages.

ui_instruct.task: On Eleanor's review desk, click remove on Sam O.'s condolence and confirm.
ui_instruct.expected_result: An are-you-sure confirmation appears before anything is deleted; after confirming, Sam O.'s 'A true friend' is gone from both the review desk and Eleanor's obituary page.

ui_instruct.task: On Marcus Webb's obituary page, type the condolence 'Thinking of the family' and submit it, then open Marcus's review desk.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The condolence shows on his obituary right away and also appears in his review desk marked unreviewed.

ui_instruct.task: Open the mortuary list page and look at its heading and the memorial cards.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The page heading is centered and rendered in a serif typeface, and each memorial's card has a cream background with 10px rounded corners and a thin gold (#C9A227) left border - not the old peru styling.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Mourners increasingly want to give, not just grieve - memorial funds with real fundraising goals turn candles into tangible support and show families how close each fund is to its target.
follow_ups.instruction: Next: memorial funds, and give each one somewhere to go - a fundraising goal per memorial: Eleanor $3,500, Marcus $1,200, Rosa $6,000, Harold $2,500, Priya $2,000, Thomas $2,000. Open every fund at $100 for each candle already lit - Rosa's starts at $2,100 - and from now on every newly lit candle automatically adds a $25 family-match pledge to that memorial's fund. Visitors can also pledge directly by typing a whole-dollar amount, $5 up to $10,000 inclusive, refusing anything outside that. Then a Funds board: every fund shows its dollars raised right next to its percent toward goal, rounded to the nearest whole percent, and the board orders funds by that percent biggest first - not by dollar amounts. Any fund at or past its goal stops showing a percent, says Goal reached instead, and moves up into its own Goal reached strip pinned above the rest of the board. And the portal-wide grand total pledged sits on top of the board.

ui_instruct.task: Open the Funds board and read the grand total, then each fund's dollars and percent going down the board.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The grand total on top reads exactly $7,500 and no fund says Goal reached yet; going down the board: Priya Nair $1,700 at 85%, Marcus Webb $900 at 75%, Eleanor Vance $1,400 at 40%, Harold Finch $900 at 36%, Rosa Delgado $2,100 at 35%, Thomas Okafor $500 at 25% - Rosa, the biggest fund in raw dollars, is second from last because the board ranks by percent toward goal, so a board ranked by dollar amounts is wrong.

ui_instruct.task: On Thomas Okafor's fund, type 4 as a pledge and try to submit it, then type 25 and submit.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The $4 pledge is refused with a message (the minimum is $5) and his total stays $500; the $25 pledge is accepted and his fund reads $525.

ui_instruct.task: On Eleanor Vance's fund, type a pledge of 10000 and submit it, then check her entry on the Funds board.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The pledge is accepted ($10,000 is exactly the allowed maximum, inclusive), her fund reads $11,400 with commas and no cents, and her board entry now says Goal reached instead of a percent and sits above all the percent-ranked funds, since $11,400 is past her $3,500 goal.

ui_instruct.task: Light a tribute candle on Priya Nair's obituary page, then open the Funds board.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Priya's fund has risen by the $25 family match to $1,725 - now 86% of her $2,000 goal - and the grand total reads $7,525; lighting a candle moves money without any pledge form.

ui_instruct.task: In the program composer, pick Eleanor Vance and switch on the include-life-story toggle.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The preview, headed Eleanor Vance (1938-2024), now lists her three milestones oldest first - 1956 Graduated Whitfield High, 1962 Married Arthur, 1990 Opened the bakery.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: After a year of candles, stories, condolences, and pledges scattered across the portal, families want a way to close the book - a reviewed, sealed record of everything the portal holds, frozen so later activity can't rewrite it.
follow_ups.instruction: One last big piece: the Family Archive. Let me pick a memorial and walk a review screen that gathers every section we hold on them - the obituary, published life story milestones, featured condolences, candle count, and fund total - with each section marked present or missing and a completeness score counting only the present ones, written as how many of the five sections are there - 4 of 5, that kind of thing. Be strict about what counts: a life story only counts once it's published, and condolences only count if one has actually been made Featured. When I confirm, the archive is sealed and lands on a new Archives page as a permanent record with its numbers frozen at sealing time - candles lit or pledges made afterwards must not change a sealed archive. And missing pieces shouldn't break anything; Thomas has no published life story, his review should just mark that section missing.

ui_instruct.task: Start a Family Archive for Eleanor Vance and look at the review screen.
ui_instruct.expected_result: It gathers 14 candles, a fund total of $1,400, and her three milestones in order 1956, 1962, 1990, and the completeness score reads 4 of 5 - the featured-condolences section is marked missing because Eleanor has condolences but none has been made Featured, so a score of 5 of 5 is wrong.

ui_instruct.task: Start a Family Archive for Thomas Okafor, go through the review screen, and seal it.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The workflow completes without breaking: his review shows 5 candles and a $500 fund, the life story section is simply marked missing rather than erroring or blocking the seal, and his sealed archive appears on the Archives page.

ui_instruct.task: Seal a Family Archive for Rosa Delgado, then light a tribute candle on her obituary page, and open the Archives page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Rosa's sealed archive still reads 21 candles and $2,100 - the numbers were frozen at sealing time - even though her live obituary page now shows 22 candles.

ui_instruct.task: On Eleanor Vance's condolence review desk, mark Ruth M.'s condolence as Featured, then start Eleanor's Family Archive and seal it.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The featured-condolences section is now marked present and lists Ruth M.'s 'She taught me to bake' - featuring a condolence over on the review desk immediately changes what the archive review gathers and seals.

ui_instruct.task: On Eleanor Vance's condolence review desk, mark Ruth M.'s condolence as Featured, then open Eleanor's obituary page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Ruth M.'s message 'She taught me to bake' now sits at the very top of the condolence list on the page identifying her as Eleanor Vance (1938-2024), wearing a gold Featured tag, above the Henderson family's and Sam O.'s messages.

target_app_summary: A year on, the memorial portal has grown from a simple obituary board into a full family remembrance platform. Visitors honor the departed with tribute candles that feed a live Honor Roll ranking, and memorial funds grow automatically from those candles plus direct pledges, each fund chasing its own goal on a Funds board ranked by percent funded rather than raw dollars. Families get real tooling: a cost estimator for planning services, a step-by-step Life Story builder with lifespan validation, a printed-program composer with a live preview, and a condolence review desk for featuring or removing guestbook entries. Discovery is handled by a multi-criteria Find a Memorial screener, everything wears the Evening Vigil restyle, and a final Family Archive workflow reviews obituary, life story, featured condolences, candles, and fund totals section by section, scores completeness, and seals a frozen-snapshot record onto an Archives page. The feature graph runs deep: candles (R2) feed the screener, funds, and archive; the Life Story (R4) feeds the screener, composer, and archive; the archive (R10) sits at the confluence of five earlier features.

instruction: Please implement a health blog website for publishing health-related articles and promoting healthy lifestyles. The website should have functionalities for publishing articles, commenting, searching, and categorizing. Users should be able to browse and search articles, post comments, and follow specific topics. Choose misty rose for global background and firebrick for all components.

ui_instruct.task: Navigate to the homepage of the health blog website and check for the presence of a search bar.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The homepage displays a functional search bar prominently, enabling users to input search queries.

ui_instruct.task: Perform a search for a specific health topic using the search bar.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The search results page displays articles related to the inputted health topic, with titles and short descriptions that match the search query.

ui_instruct.task: Access a specific article from the search results and verify the presence of a comment section.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The article page contains a comment section where users can read existing comments and write their own.

ui_instruct.task: Post a comment on an article and check the comment's appearance in the comment section.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The posted comment appears in the comment section immediately after submission, displaying correctly with the user's input.

ui_instruct.task: Browse the category section to view available health topics.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The categories are clearly listed, allowing the user to select and view articles associated with each category.

ui_instruct.task: Follow a specific health topic or category from the category list.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website confirms that the user is now following the selected topic, and it is added to a personal list or notification service.

ui_instruct.task: Verify that the website uses 'misty rose' as the background color and 'firebrick' as the component color, as specified in the design requirements.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The website has a background color of 'misty rose' and components (such as buttons, cards, headers, etc.) are styled with the color 'firebrick', accurately reflecting the design instruction.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Once the blog has real readership, both readers and the owner need to see what is resonating — a views-ranked Trending page with per-category rollups is the first analytics milestone.
follow_ups.instruction: The blog's getting real traction, so I want a Trending page that ranks our articles by views, each ranked entry showing its view and comment counts, with comment count breaking any view ties, plus a small per-category summary showing each category's article count and total views. Start me off with exactly these seven pieces: Hydration Myths Debunked (Nutrition, 1,530 words, 3,842 views, 44 comments), 5 Stretches for Desk Workers (Fitness, 400 words, 2,317 views, 9 comments), The Gut-Brain Connection (Nutrition, 890 words, 2,317 views, 27 comments), Mindful Mornings (Mental Health, 620 words, 1,204 views, 12 comments), Beat the Afternoon Slump (Nutrition, 840 words, 1,204 views, 13 comments), Why Sleep Debt Is Real (Sleep, 1,010 words, 986 views, 31 comments), and Strength Training After 40 (Fitness, 1,200 words, 750 views, 5 comments) — exactly those numbers, I'll grow the list from there. Two ground rules for everywhere in this app, now and for anything we add later: wherever an article shows up, tag it '~X min read' from its word count at 200 words a minute, always rounding up; and any time I type something invalid into a field, put a short red note right under that field instead of ignoring it or showing NaN. And when someone posts a comment on an article, the trending numbers should reflect it.

ui_instruct.task: Open the Trending page and read the ranked list from the top.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The list runs Hydration Myths Debunked, The Gut-Brain Connection, 5 Stretches for Desk Workers, Beat the Afternoon Slump, Mindful Mornings, Why Sleep Debt Is Real, Strength Training After 40 — the two 2,317-view articles ordered by comments (27 over 9) and the two 1,204-view articles likewise (13 over 12).

ui_instruct.task: Find the article Mindful Mornings anywhere it is listed and look at its read-time tag.
ui_instruct.expected_result: It reads ~4 min read — 620 words at 200 words per minute rounds up to 4, not down to 3.

ui_instruct.task: On the Trending page, look at the per-category summary entry for Nutrition.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Nutrition shows 3 articles and 7,363 total views (3,842 + 2,317 + 1,204).

ui_instruct.task: Open the article Mindful Mornings, post two comments on it — Love this and So true will do — then go to the Trending page.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Mindful Mornings now shows 14 comments and ranks above Beat the Afternoon Slump — the 1,204-view tie re-breaks the other way once its tally passes 13 — while the rest of the order is unchanged.

ui_instruct.task: Open an article from the homepage and post a comment in its comment section.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The comment appears in that article's comment section immediately after posting.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: A health blog's readers come for actionable guidance, so a live personal-targets calculator (water, BMI, steps) is the natural first interactive tool — and its saved targets seed later habit tracking.
follow_ups.instruction: Readers keep asking for something practical, so let's add a Wellness Calculator page. As I type my weight in kg and height in cm it should update live — no submit button — showing my daily water target (weight times 35 ml, displayed in liters to one decimal), my BMI to one decimal, and a daily step goal I pick by clicking an activity level: Light means 6,000, Moderate 8,500, Active 11,000. Weight only makes sense from 20 to 300 and height from 100 to 250 — anything outside that or non-numeric shouldn't produce garbage results. Also give me a save-as-my-targets button so the site remembers my daily water and step targets for later.

ui_instruct.task: On the Wellness Calculator, type 68 into the weight field and 172 into the height field.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Without pressing any button, the water target reads 2.4 L (68 × 35 = 2,380 ml) and the BMI reads 23.0.

ui_instruct.task: Type 100 into the calculator's weight field, then type an extra 0 so it reads 1000.
ui_instruct.expected_result: At 100 the water target shows 3.5 L; at 1000 a short red note appears under the weight field and the water target no longer shows a computed value.

ui_instruct.task: Click the Light activity level, then click Active.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The step goal updates immediately to 6,000 after the first click and 11,000 after the second.

ui_instruct.task: Clear the weight field and type abc into it.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A short red note appears directly under the weight field and nowhere in the results does NaN or a broken value appear.

ui_instruct.task: Open the Trending page and read the ranked list from the top.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The list runs Hydration Myths Debunked, The Gut-Brain Connection, 5 Stretches for Desk Workers, Beat the Afternoon Slump, Mindful Mornings, Why Sleep Debt Is Real, Strength Training After 40 — the two 2,317-view articles ordered by comments (27 over 9) and the two 1,204-view articles likewise (13 over 12).

follow_ups.feature_rationale: A growing blog can't run on one author — a guest-writer drafting form plus an editor review queue that publishes into the real blog is the obvious editorial milestone.
follow_ups.instruction: Time to open up to guest writers: build a Writer's Desk where someone drafts a post — a title of at least 5 characters, a category, and a body with a live word counter and a 150-word minimum to submit — and a separate Review Queue where I approve or reject each submission, with rejections requiring a short typed reason. Approved pieces go live on the blog like any other article: findable in search, listed under their category, read-time tag and all. From now on, any status shown anywhere in this app should be a little colored pill — amber for Pending, green for Approved, red for Rejected — for this and anything we build later. And preload the queue with one waiting guest piece: Stretching Before Bed, Fitness, 460 words.

ui_instruct.expected_result: Red notes appear under the title (needs at least 5 characters) and the body (below the 150-word minimum), and nothing new is added to the Review Queue.

ui_instruct.task: In the Writer's Desk body field, type the four words eat well sleep more and watch the word counter.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The counter reads 4 words and updates as each word is typed.

ui_instruct.task: Open the Review Queue as it first loads.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Exactly one submission is waiting — Stretching Before Bed, Fitness — with an amber Pending pill.

ui_instruct.task: In the Review Queue, approve Stretching Before Bed, then search for Stretching on the blog.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The search finds Stretching Before Bed as a live article tagged ~3 min read (460 words rounds up to 3, not down to 2).

ui_instruct.task: On the Wellness Calculator, type 68 into the weight field and 172 into the height field.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Without pressing any button, the water target reads 2.4 L (68 × 35 = 2,380 ml) and the BMI reads 23.0.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Readers who calculated personal targets need somewhere to track against them — a daily habit journal with a weekly rollup closes the loop between advice and practice.
follow_ups.instruction: I want to practice what we preach, so add a Wellness Journal where each day I log liters of water, hours of sleep (0 to 24, obviously), and whether I worked out — all editable after the fact. Above the log, a weekly summary: average sleep to one decimal, total water, workout count, and my progress toward the week's water goal as a percent rounded to the nearest whole number — the weekly goal being seven times the daily water target I saved in the calculator, and if I haven't saved one yet just say the goal isn't set. Fill in last week for me: Mon 2.0 L / 6.5 h / worked out, Tue 1.5 / 7 / rest, Wed 2.5 / 8 / worked out, Thu 2.0 / 5.5 / rest, Fri 1.0 / 6 / rest, Sat 3.0 / 9 / worked out, Sun 2.2 / 7.5 / rest. The summary should recalculate the moment I change any day's numbers.

ui_instruct.task: Open the Wellness Journal's weekly summary as it first loads.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Average sleep reads 7.1 h (49.5 hours over 7 days rounds to 7.1, not a truncated 7.0), total water reads 14.2 L, and the workout count reads 3.

ui_instruct.task: Edit Tuesday's sleep hours to 25.
ui_instruct.expected_result: A short red note appears under the field (sleep must be between 0 and 24) and the weekly average sleep stays at 7.1 h.

ui_instruct.task: Change Friday's water from 1.0 to 2.0.
ui_instruct.expected_result: The weekly total water immediately reads 15.2 L while average sleep stays at 7.1 h.

ui_instruct.task: In the Wellness Calculator, enter weight 68 and height 172, click the save-targets button, then open the journal's weekly summary.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Water goal progress reads 85% — 14.2 L against a 16.8 L weekly goal (7 × 2.4 L), rounded to the nearest whole percent, not 84%.

ui_instruct.task: On the Trending page, look at the per-category summary entry for Nutrition.
ui_instruct.expected_result: Nutrition shows 3 articles and 7,363 total views (3,842 + 2,317 + 1,204).

follow_ups.feature_rationale: With traffic data and a growing catalog, the owner's next job is retention — composing a newsletter digest from trending plus hand-picked articles, with an on-screen copyable output.

Every digest opens with a Trending this week block — the current top three from the Trending page in their exact order — then my picks, and at the bottom a '~N min total' line that adds up each included article's read-time minutes. follow_ups.feature_rationale: An open comment section on a popular health blog inevitably attracts spam — a moderation surface whose removals ripple correctly into article counts and the trending ranking, with a restore tray to undo mistakes, is the natural trust-and-safety milestone.
follow_ups.instruction: Spam is creeping into the comments, so I need a Moderation Center: every flagged comment listed there grouped under its article, each with a remove button, plus a remove-all button for each article's group. Removing a comment pulls it off the article and out of every count that mentions it — the article page, Trending, everywhere — and the trending order should re-settle to match. But give me a safety net too: anything I remove drops into a Recently Removed tray on the same page, and restoring one from the tray puts it straight back on its article, back into its flagged group, and bumps every count back up. Seed the queue by flagging 7 of the 13 comments already sitting on Beat the Afternoon Slump and 2 of the 31 already on Why Sleep Debt Is Real — flagging just marks an existing comment for review, so no article's comment count moves until I actually remove something.

target_app_summary: What began as a misty-rose health blog with articles, comments, search, categories and topic-following has grown into a full wellness publishing platform. Analytics arrived first: a Trending page ranking a pinned catalog of seven articles by views with comment-count tiebreaks and per-category rollups. Reader tooling grew alongside it — a live Wellness Calculator with saveable personal targets, a Wellness Journal whose weekly rollup measures progress against those saved targets, and a Reading Planner that filters the catalog by time budget and category using the app-wide rounded-up read-time rule. Editorial operations expanded through a guest Writer's Desk with a validated draft-review-publish pipeline, a Newsletter Digest Composer that leads with the live trending top three and sums per-article minutes without duplicates, and a Comment Moderation Center whose per-comment and bulk removals ripple through article counts and re-break trending ties, backed by a Recently Removed tray that can undo any of it. A personalized My Feed finally pays off topic-following (floating unread items above read ones and absorbing approved guest posts), and a final Fresh Sage restyle unifies every surface, putting every listed article on a white rounded card. The graph runs several chains deep: base articles feed trending, which feeds the digest, the planner and the moderation re-ranking, while the calculator feeds the journal and the pipeline feeds both search and the feed.

Figure reading time at 150 words a minute and always round UP to the next half minute, and show times that way everywhere in this app — like '1.5 min' — now and for anything we add later; the poems out on the blog listing should show their reading time too. If the draft is exactly 3 lines suggest 'Haiku', exactly 14 suggest 'Sonnet', anything else 'Free Verse'. target_app_summary: The little poetry blog has grown into a full poetry community platform. Writers now compose in a live Draft Studio with per-keystroke stats, save work to a Drafts shelf, and publish through a reviewed flow under a pen name. Readers applaud poems, file weighted critique scorecards, and nominate work into an editorially reviewed Weekly Spotlight. Curators assemble anthologies with computed rollups and share them as on-screen broadside previews, while a Pulse dashboard reconciles applause, critiques, and spotlight activity into a Critics' Choice list and per-form rollups. A Poet Rankings board with tie-aware ordering and a full Parchment & Ink redesign round it out. The feature graph fans out from the pinned poem seed (R3) into spotlight, critiques, anthologies, analytics, and export, with a deep chain running seed -> anthologies -> broadside export and another running seed -> spotlight -> dashboard.

target_app_summary: The simple papaya-whip link tree has grown into a full creator link-in-bio suite. The organizational spine is a sectioned link library with live/hidden visibility feeding a public tree preview; on top of that sit a click analytics dashboard, weekly per-section goals, a visitor preview simulator whose test clicks flow back into the stats and goal meters, and a weekly digest that turns the week into per-section share-of-clicks and distance-to-goal lines with a copyable plain-text version. Around the spine grew workflow tooling: a UTM campaign link builder that composes tagged URLs live and saves them into sections, a validation-heavy bulk importer with a review screen, and a delete-to-archive safety net with restore. A final visual refresh sweeps a consistent pill-and-badge design language across all five major pages. The feature graph has one deep analytics chain (sections -> analytics -> goals -> digest) plus tool and workflow branches that all read from or write into the sectioned library.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Users constantly test assumptions ('what if the batch were bigger?'); a side-by-side recompute lets them explore without touching their real variables or sheets.

target_app_summary: The one-shot expression calculator has grown into a full computation workbench. Around the original evaluate-an-expression core it gained a validated saved-variables library that expressions can reference, multi-line worksheets whose lines chain off each other and off those variables, a what-if comparator that recomputes any worksheet under typed variable overrides, and a governance flow where winning what-ifs become reviewable proposed changes that, once approved, rewrite the library and ripple through every sheet and report. Alongside that spine sit a live converter studio (units and number bases), an auto-logging calculation history with search/filter/re-run, a usage explorer that ranks variables by how often saved worksheets reference them, and an on-screen report builder for sharing a sheet's results as copyable text. A late blueprint-style restyle (paper white, navy nav, amber actions, monospace numerals) unifies all surfaces. The graph has one deep chain (calculator -> variables -> worksheets -> what-if comparator -> approval pipeline) plus analytics and export branches hanging off the variables/worksheets pair, with the converter as the lone standalone tool.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: Stages live on the shortlist while meetings accumulate on their own page, so the two drift apart silently; a per-person health check that reconciles them and names the drift keeps the pipeline honest.
follow_ups.instruction: My shortlist stages and the meetings page keep drifting out of step without me noticing. Build a Journey Health Check page that walks through everyone on my shortlist, cross-checks their stage against the meetings record, and puts exactly one status tag on each person with a plain-words reason beside it. Out of sync wins over everything else: the stage says Meeting Planned or Decision Made but there is no confirmed meeting on the books, or there is a confirmed meeting while the stage still sits at Interested or Contacted. Otherwise it's Needs a nudge when someone has no meeting activity at all — a pending proposal counts as activity, a declined one doesn't. Everyone else is On track. Recompute all of it from the live shortlist and meetings whenever I open the page.

ui_instruct.expected_result: Asha flips from On track to Needs a nudge — the declined proposal no longer counts as meeting activity — and she is not marked Out of sync, since Contacted demands no confirmed meeting.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: The app now has six major surfaces built at different times; a single Rose & Ivory language applied everywhere is what makes it feel like one product to families.
follow_ups.instruction: That lemon-chiffon-and-chocolate look is feeling dated, so rebrand everything to our new Rose & Ivory language: soft blush #FDF2F8 page backgrounds, content cards in ivory white with 12px rounded corners and a soft shadow instead of the chocolate blocks, every primary action button in deep rose #9D174D with white text, page headings centered, and any stage or score badge drawn as a fully rounded pill. This goes on every page — browse, shortlist, meetings, insights, the journey health check, budget planner, the biodata composer, all of it — don't leave a single screen in the old colors.

follow_ups.feature_rationale: The endgame of matchmaking is choosing between finalists; a side-by-side scorecard fusing compatibility, pipeline stage and meeting progress supports that decision.
follow_ups.instruction: One last big piece: a Compare & Decide page with two pickers that each select someone off my shortlist — nobody else should even appear as an option — shown side by side with their compatibility, stage, and meetings, plus a decision score for each: compatibility, plus stage points (Interested 5, Contacted 10, Meeting Planned 20, Decision Made 30), plus a 15-point bonus if they have a confirmed meeting. Crown the winner with a clear verdict line, but if the two decision scores land dead even, say it's too close to call rather than picking one.

target_app_summary: A matrimonial site that has grown from profile browsing, search and chat into a full matchmaking workbench. A live preference-driven compatibility engine scores every profile, a shortlist pipeline with stages and notes feeds a meeting proposal/confirmation workflow, and derived surfaces reconcile it all: a Match Insights dashboard, a Journey Health Check that reconciles each shortlisted person's stage with the meetings record and tags the drift, and a Compare & Decide scorecard that fuses compatibility, stage and confirmed meetings into a final verdict. Alongside the pipeline sit two self-serve tools — a live Wedding Budget Planner with saved estimates and a Biodata Composer with an on-screen copyable export — and a Rose & Ivory rebrand applied across every page. The feature graph has one deep spine (browse -> shortlist -> meetings -> health check/decide) with the compatibility engine feeding four downstream consumers, plus two low-dependency tools wired in through app-wide conventions.
